speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not think any good purpose would be served by sitting continuously. subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a series of questions to the Minister of Justice in regard to one John Wasylen-chuk of Vancouver, who has been directed to be taken from Canada under extradition. I do this because of a statement made by the Liberal leader in British Columbia, Mr. Perrault, to the effect that the Minister of Justice signed an order for the extradition of this man and, to quote what the press said, he did not know what he was doing when he signed it, that he would have signed his own death certificate.
I ask the minister, did he sign an order directing the extradition of this man several days before the habeas corpus proceedings taken by him were decided upon; what was the date of the signing of the order by the minister; what was the date when the judgment was handed down? Furthermore, did

the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice, following the signing of the order, make an attempt to stop extradition by phoning the warden of Oakalla prison yesterday, and by phoning the border officials to prevent the extradition?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions which have been put and I shall be pleased to answer them, but first I think I should give to the house the situation as it exists.
Under date October 25, 1963, the government of the United States requested extradition of John Wasylenchuk, who is charged with the crimes of robbery and murder in connection with a bank robbery in the western district of Washington, pursuant to the extradition treaty with the United States to which Canada is a party. Wasylenchuk was brought up before Mr. Justice Hutcheson of the supreme court of British Columbia for a hearing in the nature of a preliminary inquiry pursuant to the treaty and the Extradition Act. On November 14, 1963 Mr. Justice Hutcheson reported to me that he had committed Wasylenchuk for extradition pursuant to the act. He stated that the evidence before him included evidence submitted on behalf of Wasylenchuk with a view to establishing an alibi as well as evidence connecting Wasylenchuk with the alleged offence.
Next, habeas corpus proceedings were then taken on behalf of Wasylenchuk before Mr. Justice Ruttan, also of the supreme court of British Columbia, and under date of December 11, 1963 I was advised by the district registrar of the supreme court that such application had been refused. I accordingly signed an extradition warrant for Wasylenchuk's surrender to the United States authorities pursuant to the Extradition Act. It was sent out on Monday, December 16, 1963 to counsel in Vancouver acting for the United States authorities, and I understand Wasylenchuk was removed to the United States under such warrant yesterday.
In answer to one of the other questions by the right hon. gentleman, several days did expire, as he intimated in his question, between the habeas corpus proceedings being taken and the signing of the warrant. It was not until after the habeas corpus proceedings had been taken and the matter had been discussed with my officers that I signed the warrant.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
I should like to ask this question. Was the warrant signed by the minister signed before the judgment was handed down in the habeas corpus proceedings?
28902-5-389J
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: The answer to that is no; it was signed afterward.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Then would the minister also answer whether his parliamentary secretary yesterday made these communications? I ask because Mr. Perrault is reported to have stated that the Minister of Justice promised a full review early this week in a telephone conversation-

speechtext: One other question has not been answered, regarding the minister's parliamentary secretary. subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: He is of age. Let him answer.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: He is not a minister yet.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the Minister of Justice if, when he signed the surrender order for John Wasylenchuk, he was aware of the fact that he was on parole. In view of the fact that under section 11 of the Parole Act a person on parole is still deemed to be serving a sentence, and under section 24 of the Extradition Act no person who is serving a sentence can be extradited, would the minister not consider that his surrender order was illegal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. That matter was carefully gone into, both the section of the Extradition Act as well as the section

Inquiries of the Ministry of the Parole Act, and the legal advice I have received is that although a man is on parole he is still subject to extradition under the treaty and under the act. Otherwise a man who was on parole could leave the jurisdiction, go into the United States, commit an offence, come back and not be extraditable. The converse would be true with regard to a citizen of the United States who came into Canada under such circumstances. In my view the treaty which has been entered into between the two countries envisaged such a situation.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: May I ask the minister this question. Is he not bound by the Extradition Act, section 24 of which says very clearly that a person cannot be extradited if he is serving a sentence for some crime other than the one for which extradition proceedings have been taken?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: I do not agree with that interpretation of the section. The section does not say that, and the advice I have received from my officers is to the contrary. As I said earlier, my advice is that although the man is on parole he is still subject to extradition.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
A further supplementary
question. In view of the fact that Wasylen-chuk claims he was in Burnaby in 1954 at the time the offence was committed for which he is being extradited, and that any alibi he may try to establish will have to be established through witnesses in Burnaby, is any arrangement being made by the Canadian government to see that he has ample opportunity to call witnesses and to get the necessary funds to convey witnesses to the United States in order that he may receive a fair trial?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what the circumstances are with reference to the alibi, although in the statement I made earlier I pointed out that this had been considered by one of the judges. But I can tell my hon. friend that in so far as I am concerned I would be prepared to do everything possible in order that he may obtain a fair trial.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, now that there has been communication between the Minister of Justice and the parliamentary secretary, instead of asking for secondary evidence I would like to put the question to the parliamentary secretary. I ask him whether yesterday he made an attempt to stop the extradiction of Wasylenchuk by telephoning the warden or telephoning to the border.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK

I would not like to make any statement at this time without a full opportunity of discussing this with the minister, a fuller opportunity than has been possible since the minister gave his answer.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Just answer the question.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Does the parliamentary secretary not deny this? If he does not deny it, under what authority did he go behind an order that was made?

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: I would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that in view of the answer I gave the right hon. Leader of the Opposition a while ago he would at least have given me an opportunity of discussing with my parliamentary assistant what happened in my absence yesterday. subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: I noticed the two in conversation.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could I ask the minister, when he is looking into this matter and making a statement to the house, to also clarify the statement he made earlier to me; because section 24 of the Extradition Act is quite clear. It says:
A fugitive who has been accused of an offence within Canadian jurisdiction, not being the offence for which his surrender is asked, or who is undergoing sentence under a conviction in Canada, shall not be surrendered until after he has been discharged, whether by acquittal or by expiration of his sentence, or otherwise.
It seems to me that is, for legal terminology, unusually explicit. I hope the minister will clarify this point because it would seem, on the face of it, that the surrender order which he signed is clearly illegal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is simply repeating the statement which he made earlier. When I do anything in the Department of Justice I accept the advice of the legal officers and, unfortunately, not of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I must repeat what I said to him a while ago, that the advice I was given in so far as this section is concerned was that it did not apply under the circumstances.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: All I am asking the minister to do is, when he makes his statement-

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Order, please. We have had quite a full discussion, and I think the Minister of Justice seized the point.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: Will Your Honour not give me a chance to say what I was going to ask the minister to do?

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: This is not the time to make an argument. We have discussed the matter on two occasions this morning.

subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: I am not making an argument, Mr. Speaker. I am just asking a question. I am asking the minister a question and saying that as a member of the house I have the right to some explanation from him. The mere fact that he tells me his law officers have advised him is not sufficient. I am asking the minister whether he will be kind enough to tell the house, when he makes his statement, how he reconciles the opinion which was given to him by his law officers with section 24 of the Extradition Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: JOHN WASYLENCHUK
speechtext: I do not think there will be any difficulty about that, Mr. Speaker, and if the hon. member will just hold his patience, perhaps tomorrow I will be able to make a statement on the matter.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES IN LABOUR DISPUTE AT GRANDE PRAIRIE, ALTA.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have but a few remarks to make at this stage, because I do not want to delay the business of the house too much.
Our Liberal friends have made so many promises when they were in the opposition that I cannot let an opportunity slip by without reminding them a few of their election promises and urging them to carry them out.
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) reminds me that this being Christmas time, it would be the most appropriate time for the Minister of Agriculture to carry out his promises.
Mr. Chairman, referring to the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963, we remember that at that time, the Liberal candidates were travelling throughout our ridings, reminding the farmers that agriculture was in a stage of stagnation, but that they had all the solutions to their problems.
No wonder the voters were deceived by these fine words; but now they ask them to keep those promises.
I am one of those who now intend to ask those people to keep their promises.
One of the main promises was that eastern farmers would have a minister from the east. We remember that at the beginning of the session the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), now leader of the house, requested the house to do things quickly, in order that we may appoint a minister of agriculture for the east as soon as possible. So it is surprising now to see that his former impatience to proceed in this field has turned into unending delays, since this appointment is even postponed until the next session.
Mr. Chairman, in that field, we are facing two contradictory positions on the part of our friends on the other side, which well indicates the extent of their sincerity when they speak about farmers, for if we go back to April 8 last, we find that very little has been done in the field of agriculture to improve the condition of the farmer.
As soon as they came to power, they introduced a measure which had baleful results, especially for the farmers in my district. As soon as he took over as Minister of Agriculture, the first thing he thought advisable to do was to remove the 25-cent premium per hundred pounds of milk granted to farmers who sold their milk to plants.
We have here an idea of the extent of the damage caused to farmers in my constituency, if we consider that after the Conservative government established that premium, farmers
Sup p ly-A griculture
in St. Hyacinthe-Bagot benefited by the amount of $1,576,222.
As concerns the farmers in the province, the premium represents an amount of nearly $21 million they would have received during the years that measure applied.
It is difficult to understand that people wishing to help the agricultural class find nothing better to do than removing that premium and depriving the farmers, both in my constituency and in the province, of such an essential revenue. It must not be forgotten that at least 40 per cent of the farmers' income is derived from the dairy industry.
They had a right to expect different conduct on the part of the minister.
If he wishes to know what the farmers think of the present government's agricultural policy, he just has to pay them a visit. He will see that his popularity and that of the Liberal government is going down constantly month by month.
Mr. Chairman, you can also have an idea of the Liberal party's concern for farmers when you consider that at the election of last April, 15 farmers were eliminated at Liberal conventions.
In the June 1962 election, Mr. Jean Baptiste Lemoyne had run in my own riding and was reported to be a future minister of agriculture in a Liberal cabinet. When one considers that he was turned down at the convention during the 1963 election campaign, the degree of sincerity of the Liberal party towards farmers can readily be appreciated. I believe that the Liberals lost no time in removing that premium as soon as they came into power so as to punish the rural ridings for supporting the Conservative party.
The hon. gentleman who aspires to become minister of agriculture is somewhat guilty himself because he spared no effort to eliminate from this house a genuine farmer, Mr. Alfred Belzile who had accomplished a great deal here. He was known by all members of the house as a genuine farmer who made a valuable and worth-while contribution whenever agricultural matters were being considered in the house.
I must tell the candidate to the ministry that his attitude was at complete variance with that of the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Tremblay) because when he was asked questions, he did not give the impression, like his successor, that they did not deserve any consideration.
During these last weeks, I directed questions to the hon. minister and he gave the impression that he felt he was too far above the common herd to reply. If he wants a piece of advice for his own information and his own future good, and if he really wants to do

Supp ly-A griculture
something for the farmers, he should have a little more humility and consider himself as part of this world.
Mr. Chairman, during the 1962 and 1963 elections, and also during past sessions when our friends opposite sat on opposition benches, they had answers to all questions and rose one after the other to deplore the lot made to the farmers by the Conservative government.
But it is a recognized fact that the Conservative party and particularly the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) have given the farmers much more during six years of Conservative administration than they had been given by the Department of Agriculture while its activities were directed by the hon. Mr. Gardiner.
Those gentlemen said in their speeches that new leadership had to be given to the milk products industry and steps taken to have milk distributed in the schools. Well, Mr. Chairman, what do you have since those people have come to power? Are they carrying out the policy which they advocated in the past? Absolutely not. We are not distributing more milk in the schools than formerly. Perhaps those people have realized that we were encroaching on a field which did not come under their jurisdiction.
This is further evidence that they should have tackled the problem with more sincerity, that they should have studied it before speaking; thus, they would not have ventured in fields where they are completely lost.
When we were in power, the hon. member for QuAppelle had legislation passed to help particularly, the dairy farmer in the province of Quebec and eastern Canada. In order to promote butter consumption we granted a reduction of 12 cents per pound of butter to the consumer. This has represented a considerable incentive to butter sales and today, this commodity sells much more than formerly.
Mr. Chairman, there is something disturbing in the fact that the subsidy may be withdrawn altogether, as pointed out in an article I was reading a few weeks ago in La Terre de chez-nous. Is anything being done now to condition the farmer and the consumer in that respect?
I think it is my duty, in my capacity as representative of a semi-rural and semi-urban riding, to urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) and, if I may, the next minister of agriculture, to use all their energies and influence to have this subsidy maintained and not abolished.
Having said this Mr. Chairman, may I present to the Minister of Agriculture, to the aspiring Minister of Agriculture, as well as

to all my friends in the opposition, my best wishes for the year 1964, but I wish them a short political life.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: You are the friends in the opposition.

subtopic: ACTIVITIES IN LABOUR DISPUTE AT GRANDE PRAIRIE, ALTA.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make to give the minister a chance to reply afterwards.
I wish to start by bidding the minister good luck in his new functions.
Then I should like to bring to the attention of the house a brief addressed to the present Minister of Agriculture by the corporation of agronomists of the province of Quebec. Here are a few excerpts:
My dear Minister,
The corporation of agronomists of the province of Quebec wishes to draw to your kind attention the situation of the agronomists who are employed by the federal Department of Agriculture in the province of Quebec. Several of these federal agronomists are not fairly classified and remunerated. considering the responsibilities attached to the duties they have to perform.
A little further down, it says this:
Certain functions such as the inspection of crops should be the exclusive responsibility of agronomists with good knowledge of phytopathology and entomology acquired at the university. At one time, the veterinarian responsible for a sub-district earned exactly the same salary as the agronomist of the federal Department of Agriculture in the production service. Today, this veterinarian gets an average of $1500 more in some cases. Yet, the agronomist's responsibilities are quite as important. A salary scale which discriminates against a profession in favour of others coming under the same employer, in spite of equal responsibilities, could not be considered as fair.
This letter that I have not read in full bears the signature of Mr. T. Mongeon, agronomist and secretary general of the corporation of agronomists of the province of Quebec.
I ask the minister and his departmental officials to look into those suggestions, in order that the agronomists in the province of Quebec, and even in other provinces, may be treated as fairly as the veterinarians and a complete review be made so that their professional status may enable them to receive a salary equivalent to those paid in other fields of agriculture throughout the country.
Mr. Chairman, the federal Department of Agriculture is one of the most important in Canada, and at the same time one of the most complex.
May I take this opportunity to congratulate the present deputy minister, Dr. Barry, who discharges his responsibilities so well.
I think, Mr. Chairman, the associate deputy minister of agriculture, Mr. Chagnon, who is a qualified man familiar with the problems of agriculture, particularly those concerning

eastern Canada, should have wider responsibilities in the federal Department of Agriculture, because the present deputy minister, Dr. Barry, assumes in my opinion so many responsibilities and does so much work that it is impossible for him, even if he so wishes, to give special consideration to all the problems.
I believe it would be in the interest of the federal Department of Agriculture, that is in the interest of the agricultural class, to find a means or method of sharing responsibilities, so that Mr. Chagnon, who has been appointed lately associate deputy minister of agriculture, would share equal responsibilities with Dr. Barry.
It is not my intention to blame anybody in saying this. On the contrary. I have always greatly admired the officials of the Department of Agriculture, but I believe there is reason to divide executive responsibilities at that level.
I should also like to make a few remarks in connection with federal experimental farms. The problems that arise there are not new; they are of long standing.
To correct the situation in the province of Quebec, it is imperative to take the necessary steps to provide the experimental farms with a greater budget and with more agricultural technicians, doctors in agricultural sciences and agronomists.
I know that agronomists are scarce in French Canada at present, because the Quebec government has attracted a large number of them by offering high salaries. In other words, the provincial government has fine agronomists in its employ.
I submit that the Department of Agriculture should give special consideration to the problem so as to find in Quebec agronomists to fill jobs first in Ottawa and, in the second place, at research stations in the province.
I would strongly advise the Minister of Agriculture to ask one of his deputy ministers to go to the faculty of agronomy at Laval University to explain to the students the federal government's need for agronomists, so that agricultural technicians may come and take the place to which they are entitled within the federal Department of Agriculture.
Mr. Chairman, I come back now to the subject of experimental farms. I have here figures and statistics but for the time being I have no intention of quoting them. However, I should like that special attention be given to the federal experimental farm of L'Assomp-tion. I have here a report prepared by the local chamber of commerce of L'Assomption area. This report was prepared by Mr. Richard
Sup p ly-A griculture
Bordeleau, who is the director of the experimental farm in that area; he is very competent and he has prepared this report with the co-operation of officers of the chamber of commerce in an effort to find a way to fill the vacancies in the federal experimental farm of L'Assomption area.
Let me quote a few excerpts from the resolutions passed by the chamber of commerce of L'Assomption on June 2, 1963.
Whereas the number of stations for agricultural research as of April 1962 represented 21.3 per cent of the Canadian total for Ontario and 17 per cent for Quebec;
Whereas the number of professionals engaged in that research represented to this date 17 per cent of the total for Ontario and 9.3 per cent of the total for Quebec.
This submission of the chamber of commerce goes on along this line and it is an excellent brief. As I said, we ought to try by all possible means to compensate this deficiency, this lack of agronomists at the federal level.
Those are the few remarks I wanted to make at this time.
I wish that in 1964, the Minister of Agriculture will be able to implement the brief of the corporation. I would be glad if, later on, the minister would be able to comment on it and tell us whether he thinks that the suggestions to be found in the brief are good.
To conclude, I also ask the government to fully consider the problems of the farmers in the east and in British Columbia. As we have said already, the work to be done is tremendous and the field is broad, but I know that by co-operating and working together, we will succeed in raising the revenue of the farming class in eastern Canada as well as in British Columbia.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to prolong the debate on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, but I feel it is my duty as a farmer from western Canada to seek clarification from the Minister of Agriculture of some of the policies that were advocated by the Liberals during the election campaign. Now that we are coming to the end of a session and also to the end of 1963 I believe it is the responsibility of the Minister of Agriculture to give us answers to some of the questions in which the western farmers are very much interested.
During the time the previous government was in office they were very much concerned about a two price system for wheat, and on three occasions during those years acreage payments were made in lieu of a two price system amounting to approximately $40 million a year. This did not seem to be acceptable so far as the Liberal platform was concerned and they recommended $2 per bushel

Supp ly-A gricu Iture
for No. 1 wheat, with the idea that the difference between the price farmers are now getting and $2 should be regarded as in the nature of a two price system for wheat consumed domestically. We have not heard anything more about this since this parliament started. The government also promised that in addition to a price of $2 per bushel for No. 1 wheat the prices of other grades would be adjusted accordingly, and I should like the minister to deal also with this point.
The second promise the Liberal party made had to do with the initial delivery of wheat. They promised that on the initial quota of 300 bushels a price of $3 or $4 per bushel- I cannot remember which-would be paid. The farmers of the west would like to know what the policy of the government is with regard to these promises. I must say that we have had a good crop and have been able to sell more wheat than in other years. Nevertheless, over the years the farmers have always asked for a two price system for western wheat, and before the session ends we would like to know from the Minister of Agriculture what the Liberal policy is in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to take only a few minutes, because I realize everyone wants to get the estimates through as soon as possible. However, I do want to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that for some time, over a year, I was denied the opportunity to get reports made by the economics division of the Department of Agriculture with respect to the agricultural potential of the area affected by the proposed high Arrow lakes dam project and also with respect to the effect on agriculture of certain proposed dams in the east Kootenay area. Finally I got a copy of the report on the Arrow lakes quite recently from the deputy minister, Mr. Barry.
I simply want to say that if the economics division of the Department of Agriculture is going to publish reports as inaccurate as this one the people of Canada will have very little confidence in their reliability. This report mentions that there has been no detailed soil survey, and this indicates that the persons who made the report cannot know very much about the agricultural potential of the area. I am not going to read it because it will be dealt with by very informed people before the committee on external affairs when the Columbia treaty is presented to the committee. However, I can tell the minister I have one neighbour about 40 miles north of our	home who	shipped$40,000 worth	of cattle	last	year.	Anotherneighbour 40	miles to	the	south	shipped$37,000 worth	of cattle	and	fruit,	and one
little community which has about 80 acres in

fruit shipped $60,000 worth last year. There are only three areas in Canada where peaches can be grown, the Niagara peninsula, the Okanagan, and sections of the west Kootenay district.
To indicate how inaccurate this report is, I wrote a letter to our retired district agriculturalist and horticulturalist, a man I have known for many years and who has had long time experience in the Kootenays. This is what he has to say with respect to the report: Dear Mr. Herridge,
Your letter along with the preliminary report on the agricultural potentials of the area affected by the proposed high Arrow lakes dam project, received a few days ago. I was glad to hear from you and to receive this report. The report is very inaccurate and misleading in many respects. Where they got the information in this report is hard to say, as they have not given the district a true picture and facts as to agricultural production as a whole covering the area. There is nothing wrong with the soil, some of the best in the province, excellent climate, and water can be had for irrigation if required. Most kind of fruits can be grown in the area and can compete with the best grown in British Columbia. One of the best sections in the west Kootenay district for future development in fruit, field crops, hay crops, alfalfa and raising of livestock. Tree fruit diseases is not a serious factor in this area. New sprays that have been developed in the last few years makes it possible to control these orchard diseases with much less work and sure of success in the operation.
I sure would hate to see this beautiful agricultural valley flooded. We will need the land to produce food and a place to live.
Yours very truly,
E. C. Hunt
I have another letter from the manager of B.C. Tree Fruits Limited, who is preparing a brief and who is appalled at the inaccuracy of this so-called report on the potential of the area.
About a year or so ago I was informed of another report and I tried to get it without success. I wrote to the deputy minister of agriculture on November 26 last but I have not received a reply yet. In that letter I said:
I would also appreciate receiving a copy of the memorandum regarding the effect on agriculture of construction of reservoirs on the Columbia and Kootenay rivers between Luxor and Dorr dams, Department of Agriculture-July 14, 1960.
My complaint is first simply that apparently the departments of the government, or branches of certain departments, are making their reports to fit the political requirements of the government of the day. Now, we want accuracy; we must be fair about this.
My second complaint it that members of this house have been denied this information when members of the press and some other persons have seen these reports. That is what I object to very strongly indeed, and I bring this question to the minister's attention in

the hope that this information in both instances-that is, both reports-will be made available to all members of the house. I also ask that his economics division make a further study of this question, rather than the superficial one they have made in which they admit there has been no detailed soils survey and on the spot survey. I say without any hesitation that this report on the Arrow lakes section from an agriculturist's point of view is no credit to the economics division of the Department of Agriculture.

The reason I suggested that this information should not be made available is that I have quite a bit of experience of what happens when a flock of sheep is slaughtered because of scrapie. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle knows all that is involved, and the reason for a slaughter policy.
Since 1955 we have destroyed something like 14,000 sheep and 396 individual people have been involved in nine provinces. Usually the owner of a slaughtered flock has sold breeding stock or rams into four or five different provinces, and there is a belief that scrapie is an inherited disease. That being the case the animals which have been sold are followed, and in the interval probably one of them may have been sold to a farmer in Prince Edward Island. That animal is traced and destroyed, and this creates a problem for the man who purchased it because it makes it difficult for him to sell other sheep to his neighbours and sheep breeders. Even though the animal which has been destroyed may have been with his flock just a few days and may not have associated with his other sheep, breeders stay away from that flock for a long time afterwards. There is a stigma on the flock.
If the hon. member wants these names produced we will be glad to produce them, but that is the reason I thought it better not to produce them. There are some 134 people involved in Ontario alone and it was in the interests of protecting these people that I made the answer I did.

Mr. Chairman, on this matter of scrapie we may as well finish the discussion on item 1. I had intended to raise it on vote No. 75. As all hon. members will know, I put a question on the order paper, No. 1,730, several weeks ago asking for exactly the information that the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is now seeking; that is, respecting the payment of compensation for the slaughtering of sheep that were diagnosed as having scrapie. I did not realize at the time that

Supply-A gricu Iture
so many breeders had in fact been paid under the act; I did not realize that it encompassed such a large area. As a matter of fact there are 393 breeders in nine provinces. This information is recorded on page 6054 of Hansard.
The reason I requested that the wording of that question be changed was simply to protect innocent breeders from having the value of their herds brought down because they had been named, when they did not actually have their herds exposed to scrapie for a long period of time; and of course, as has been pointed out, there is not complete agreement among the veterinarians even now as to whether this disease is hereditary.
In the question I put to the Minister of Agriculture, which was answered on December 18, I asked him to point out, without giving the names, those breeders who had received compensation more than once under the scrapie slaughter and compensation program. We see there are 13 such breeders. When I looked at the answer I found there was one sheep breeder, No. 7, who received $50,000 in September of 1959, and in July of 1963 he received $24,000. In other words, about $75,000 went to this one sheep breeder. Then further down a breeder is listed as No. 9. We find he has been paid three times, and in those three times he has received $143,000. In other words these two breeders have received about 35 per cent of all the money that has been paid out under the program in ten years of operation.
I think the Department of Agriculture, if they are going to continue this scrapie program-and in view of the information I have I think it should be taken off the list as a named disease for which compensation will be paid-these two breeders should be notified that if they want to get back into the sheep business they do so at their own risk. We have paid them well over $200,000 now. I understand there may even have been difficulty in arriving at the evaluation figures. There may be validity in the health of animals branch making compensation and demanding the slaughter of certain animals in order to eradicate disease, but in my opinion scrapie is a disease which they do not know exactly how to diagnose. As a matter of fact, in the United Kingdom they do not name this disease as something that can be eradicated by slaughter methods, and there is no compensation program. They destroy the actual animals that have the disease but they do not go back through the whole progeny of these animals and destroy them, because they are not satisfied that this is helpful; they are not even satisfied that it is contagious.
I intended raising this matter on vote 75, Mr. Chairman, but I think the time is long

past for our health of animals branch in Canada to get in touch with the health of animals branch in the United States and see if they cannot reach some kind of agreement to take scrapie off the list; because the fact is that this slaughter and compensation for slaughter is destroying the purebred sheep industry in Canada. I would urge the minister to take this action as soon as possible.

A shift to cheese production from butter has helped provide the dairy industry with the most optimistic situation experienced in many years, President J. M. Hartwick of the national dairy council of Canada said yesterday.

"Total consumption of all types of cheeses in 1963 will be well in excess of 155 million pounds," Mr. Hartwick said. Per capita consumption on the domestic market this year will reach about 81 pounds, an increase of nearly 4 pounds per person in the last 15 years.

Mr. Chairman, I had no intention of saying anything on item 1, but after listening to some of the assertions made a few minutes before the one o'clock recess, I feel

it my duty to remind the house once again of something I have referred to on several occasions-at least twice, on May 23 and October 15 of this year. While the minister was absent as well as all the other members of the cabinet, I mentioned that the price of milk in the province of Quebec was lower this year than last year.
During the speech I made on October 15, 1963, I quoted figures from:
Report on milk products marketing, marketing information section, Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, Ont.
I said that, in August 1962, according to the figures published by the Department of Agriculture, the price of milk for cheese ranged from $2.85 to $3.05 and that this year, for the same month, it ranged from $2.85 to $2.97. That means a decrease of 8 cents per hundredweight for the farmers and producers in my province. We noticed that decrease in each of our ridings.
Before the adjournment, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) gave the names of the farmers who were getting less for their milk this year than last year.
Again, I would like to repeat what I said last May 23 by showing you, for instance, that a farmer in my riding, Mr. Jean Louis La-charite, living in Petit St. Esprit, Nicolet, received this year $2.78 per hundredweight of milk, whereas he received last year $2.76 plus 25 cents per hundredweight in subsidies.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) wants to make inquiries, he only has to write to J. J. Joubert Limitee, in Nicolet, and he will be told that they pay 23 cents per hundredweight less than last year.
I do not want to put on the record all the payments made by cheese factories that I have with me, but I do want to say this to the house. We are the representatives of rural counties, elected to this house to champion the interests of our farmers. I submit that when an hon. member gets up to put on the record of the house a given problem, which entails losses amounting to millions of dollars to the Quebec farmers, members should at least have the common decency to listen to him, to read his speeches and to study them.
Mr. Chairman, those figures are not the work of my imagination; they have been supplied to me by the Department of Agriculture itself. It was not my intention today to point out again their appropriateness. I thought that we would have the opportunity to raise the question in the committee on agriculture.
Therefore, in view of those facts, I am of the opinion that this question will have to be solved in this house, because the way the committee is sitting now, with 12, 15 and 18 Conservative and only two or three Liberal

members, we realize that those members are not interested in the problems of agriculture in eastern Canada, and we do not trust the Liberal government for the solution of our difficulties.
As I was saying, the price of milk is lower this year. Even if, in August 1962, the price of cheese was 32.2 cents a pound and the subsidy was only 25 cents per hundred pounds, the price of milk was lower, this year, whereas the price of cheese was 35.3 cents a pound and the subsidy, 30 cents per hundred pounds.
If you consider that from nine to nine and a half pounds of cheese can be produced from 100 pounds of milk, it means that there should be an increase of 25 to 30 cents per hundred pounds of milk. Moreover, whereas a subsidy increase of 5 cents per hundred pounds was provided before, we did not get that increase this year.
The other day I asked the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Tremblay) and the Minister of Agriculture to give special consideration to that problem.
We are now at the end of the session, and indeed at the end of the year, and this problem concerning the farmers of my province seems to have been disregarded.
On May 23 last, when I pointed out the difference between the subsidies of 14| cents per pound of fat and of 12 cents per pound of butter, I was told that those figures were incorrect. I still remember that some hon. members even went so far as to contradict me. But today, they must be saying: He was right, those prices are lower.
I should not want to see the estimates of the Department of Agriculture passed by the house without the minister giving us a clear and definite answer on the matter, and not only the type of answer we have been getting since last May: "The price of milk is higher and those who claim that it is lower than it was last year are wrong".
Well, Mr. Chairman, those are the figures given by the Minister of Agriculture which confirm that I was right to say that this year, the farmers are in such a situation on account of the inertia of the Liberal government, and the inaction of the 46 Quebec Liberal members who do not even bother to attend the meetings of the committee on agriculture-we, the 12 to 15 Conservative members, have to wait almost half an hour to have a quorum of 20. We only have to note the attendance in the committee on agriculture to find out that there are only two or three Liberal members, one or two out of 46, while we are only eight Conservative members from the province of Quebec and we are at least three to sit on this committee to discuss farm problems.

We do not make long speeches nor do we give lectures, but these problems exist and they have to be solved. It is important that this money which belongs to the farmers of Quebec and of the whole Canada goes back to them.
I should also like to mention that this year a 10 cents a pound subsidy is paid on casein, at a cost to the federal government of $2,300,000. The price for casein last year-and no Liberal member is aware, I think, of the casein price last year-was 20 cents on the Montreal market. This year, with the 10 cents a pound subsidy, the casein price is 21 cents a pound, that is an increase of 1 cent a pound to offset the 10 cents a pound subsidy. Now, this means that $2,300,000 go to 13 Canadian casein producers, 11 of whom are from the province of Quebec.
What I am saying about the price of milk used for the production of cheese also applies to the price of milk used for the production of powdered milk.
I should like to remind my Liberal friends once more that when they were in power, in 1953, the price of milk used for the production of cheese fluctuated between $2.23 and $2.40; $2.31 and $2.40, in 1954; $2.21 and $2.48, in 1955 and $2.45 and $2.76, in 1956. But under the Conservative administration, the price fluctuated between $2.73 and $3.00, in 1957; $2.87 and $3.15, in 1958; $2.80 and $3.16, in 1959; $2.85 and $3.12, in 1960; $2.80 and $2.95, in 1961 and $2.85 and $3.05, in 1962.
Following the return to office of my Liberal friends and the promises they had made- such promises as the hon. member for Lotbi-niere (Mr. Choquette) used to make when he went around the province of Quebec saying: "I know about eggs, dairy industry"-the price of milk went down immediately to $2.97, that is a reduction of eight cents per cwt., because the government wanted to save the taxpayers from $6 to $8 million.
Now, eastern farmers, will not even get the income required to maintain their operations, if this situation continues.

I will conclude this statement now, but I should like to hear a reply from the Minister of Agriculture. Let him not simply tell us, as he has told us three, four, five, six or seven times before, that the price of milk is higher. I want to hear him explain why farmers in the province of Quebec are losing millions of dollars this year because the price of milk is lower than it was last year and because the prices of cheese, skimmed milk and all the other milk products should be higher by at least 20 cents or 30 cents a hundred pounds.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the opportunity at this time to express my views on the situation of agriculture in general but especially on the conditions of farmers in eastern Canada, in the province of Quebec and more particularly in the riding of Compton-Frontenac which I have the honour to represent in the house.

Supply-Agriculture
First, I should like to stress the part played by agriculture in our national economy. Without getting into all the details, I would say that, with the exception of the western provinces, agriculture has known better days in Canada.
In 1962-63, the federal government provided $161 million for agriculture. In 1963-64, the estimates of the department have been raised by $11,213,360 for a grand total of $172,221,160. On the whole, that is not even enough to settle several major problems which face our farmers.
It is very difficult, according to our set of values, to reconcile some figures, to account for the fact for instance, that national defence appropriations are nine times higher than those of the Department of Agriculture.
We are given some information about the farmers' situation which leaves us sceptical, because it does not often reflect the actual plight of our farmers. For instance, La Presse published the following item on May 28 last:
In 1962, farmers had a record income. But when the reasons for this 6.6 per cent increase over last year's income are looked into, it is soon realized that western farmers are those who benefited from it. We are happy about this, but the problems of eastern farmers remain unchanged, the solutions offered are often unpractical or still based on the work of three generations to come.
On the other hand, a press release from the association for the expansion and protection of agriculture in eastern Canada incorporated, dated January 1963, bears the following title:
Income of Canadian farms falls during the year.
Let me quote the first paragraph of that press release:
Canada is at the bottom of the list of countries where the farmers' income has decreased last year. According to the annual report of the United Nations Food and Agricultural Organization, the decrease reached 24 per cent. This has brought the net income of Canadian farms in 1961 to its lowest level since 1945. However, the cash income of farmers increased, owing to the sale of the stocks of the preceeding years, according to that report.
Here again, the marketing of those stocks concerns western farmers. To quote another sentence of the press release:
It is difficult to reconcile the sad position of eastern farmers with the fact that our country should be first in agricultural prosperity.
I leave it to the hon. members of the western provinces to enlighten us on the various aspects of the agricultural situation in their region; thanks to the marketing of their wheat in the last two years, western farmers are sitting pretty, while in the east, most of our farmers are going through a very critical period.

The Economiste agricole of August 1963, on page 75, has this to say about farm income:
For the first quarter of 1963, the farm income in Canada reached $654.7 million, as against $596.1 million for the first quarter of 1962, and $661.3 million for the corresponding quarter of 1961. These estimates include cash income from the marketing of agricultural products, payments made by the Canadian wheat board on the grain crops of previous years, prepayments on grain stored on western farms and deficiency payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, but do not include the supplementary payments.
The increase in income during the first quarter of 1963 is due mostly to the increase in proceeds from the sale of wheat, coarse grains, potatoes, cattle, calves and poultry products as well as to larger payments made by the Canadian wheat board on grain crops of previous years. There was also a slight increase in prices for rye, fruits, vegetables, tobacco, and dairy products.
It is quite easily seen that with a few exceptions, the increase radically ignores Quebec farmers and most of the eastern farmers.
The same situation prevails at all levels of farming for eastern farmers, and in particular for Quebec farmers.
Looking for a few minutes at the 18th annual report of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, we note, for instance, that as far as loans for the purchase of farm implements are concerned, Quebec is not among the four provinces which registered a raise in the loans for purchase of tractors. Once again, with the exception of Quebec and Ontario, there was an increase in all provinces of combines financing. For the purchase and financing of several other farm implements, Quebec always has the honour of being in the last place.
As far as loans for farm buildings are concerned, Quebec is conspicuous again, holding the last place. The situation is the same as regards loans for the purchase of cattle.
What is wrong in Quebec?
With your permission, I shall use a few examples taken in my own constituency to illustrate quite briefly the unfortunate lot of our farmers. First of all, Quebec agriculture has always been in a different context and generally does not know the specialization which characterizes western farmers.
Our farmers who are not very prosperous very often do not have the basic credit required nor the necessary security to secure loans. They often need guidance. On that matter, the federal as well as the provincial authorities do not seem to be capable to cooperate, and if the problems are taken into consideration, solutions are viewed in the framework of a regionalism which does not take into account geographic, physical, social and economic characteristics of a given sector in a region.

It is true comprehensive studies on problems are necessary to arrive at a guidance which may be useful to the majority. But, here again, if I refer to Mr. Brownstone, volume 3, page 59, chapter "Land Maintenance and Improvement" in Resources for Tomorrow, I read the following:
Within each government jurisdiction there are problems of a different order. Effective land maintenance and improvement requires integrated, or at least co-ordinated effort from a number of directions. At the federal level, and in many of the provinces, such integration and co-ordination exists (if at all) only at cabinet level. The federal legislative-administrative organization for the use and management of agricultural resources is administered by ten departments. Complete integration may not be possible, but greater integration combined with effective co-ordination is a realistic objective.
However, the fact remains it should be possible for our farmers, and here I refer particularly to those in my constituency of Compton-Frontenac, to obtain the services of consultants to study their particular problems, and to see thereby the production potential and the economic soundness of farms which cannot support the farmers if they do not experience some specialization.
On page 23, dealing with agricultural resources, I read the following:
There is no doubt research on soil sciences, animal and plant genetics and agricultural practices may increase production. The proof was obtained on a large scale.
But our farmers are caught, and they have to live and support their families. The primo vivere is found here as everywhere else. They have to expatriate themselves to the United States where they find work as labourers and lumbermen and they do not even benefit from the unemployment insurance when they come back. That is the pitiful situation of our old regions in Quebec. In Le Devoir of November 28, my attention was drawn to an article:
Mr. Paul E. Lachance stated at Roberval that farmers cannot be at the same time farmers and foresters.
Our forests have always brought additional revenues but for the average farmer, they cannot give him a living and often they prevent preparatory works that should be done in order to make the land produce as it should.
We have great projects in existence, ARDA for instance, which in the long run may give tangible results.
What our farmers need, at least in my district, is to know if, for instance, it would be economical to start hog, poultry or cattle breeding, or else, if on account of special factors, truck-gardening would offer a solution, the blueberry culture could be considered, and our farmers could draw some
Supp ly-A griculture
revenue from reforestation. Those are all possibilities, but, the very idea often makes the individual farmer shrink from fear.
Our farmers should be able to borrow without having to pay interest rates they cannot meet; they should be able to purchase tractors at low prices. When we consider for one moment the money spent for the production of armoured cars and other motorized weapons which after all will never be used in our time, it is inconceivable that the government cannot do anything to provide for the equipment of those who are the very foundation of the country's survival.
Therefore, I appeal to the government to restore the value of agriculture in eastern Canada, to take concrete and efficient steps so that our farmers may earn a decent living and not have to keep trying to make both ends meet. Above all, I ask the government not to get muddled up in piles of dust-gathering reports and red tape which only serve to get everybody mixed up and do not help solve anything in the end.
Members of the cabinet, the situation is alarming, there is a revolt brewing among our farm people, and not without cause. It is more than time to get some action. Our farmers are not asking for favours. They have shown themselves ready to work. What they need is tools and capital, and leadership as well. We are waiting impatiently for a realistic piece of legislation, one which will not give everything to the same people. We agree that it is important that agriculture be prosperous in western Canada but the eastern farmer also has the right to live, not as an overworked second class citizen but in all the dignity he has managed to retain in spite of the fact that the government has neglected him.
The Canadian confederation will cease to be a Utopia the day the plowed fields bear their fruits from the Atlantic to the Pacific and will not just crowd the Rockies, unaware even of the existence of the eastern farmers and, in particular, of Quebec farmers.
As the spokesman for the farmers of the riding of Compton-Frontenac, I ask the government to take action before it is too late. These are not threats but rather the result of findings which are only partly translated by the few ideas I have tried to express here.

I understand that much of the 1963 crop has not been sold as yet, and some of it is going sour in the storage rooms of farmers or local co-operatives. The maple sugar business would be good if the government would go out and see if they could not get greater markets. At the moment many farmers are closing down their maple sugar business because it is not profitable; in fact at the end of the year they are in the hole to the tune of approximately $1 a tree.
I was at one meeting at which the yearly budget was presented, and it ran somewhere around $5 million. I would not have accepted a budget such as that. During the past five or six years maple sugar producers have tried to ascertain the market price for their product. They know what they are receiving

for it, but they do not know the retail price. At the moment the producers receive from $2.35 to $2.50 per gallon for No. 1 syrup. I am sure if you bought that syrup from a store

I am not talking about the immediate vicinity in which it is produced-you would not pay $2.50 for that syrup. There seems to be some sort of control over this market to such an extent that syrup was not bought this year but left in the storage houses to go sour. Then, too, there is no relationship between the purchase price of the syrup and the return the farmer receives, considering the amount of work he has put into it.
I would ask the minister, instead of paying subsidies, to look into the situation and see if he can straighten it out. A lot of sugar businesses are closing down, and production of maple sugar is a typical business in eastern Canada. In fact production of maple sugar elsewhere in the world is rare. It would be a good thing if we got a larger market in Canada for maple syrup. We should stop buying extract which is supposed to be maple syrup. We pay a ridiculous price for artificial syrup; it is dearer than the pure product, yet the farmers cannot sell the real maple syrup produced on their farms. I would ask the minister to take this matter into consideration, and if he has any statement to make I would like to hear it, as would also the producers of maple syrup.
Another point I want to raise concerns the control which is developing over the sale of beef cattle in my area as well as in other regions, from what I have heard. This has developed as a result of brucellosis and tuberculosis in cattle. We are attempting to classify cattle in different areas and prevent their transportation from one area to another. A control is exercised in this way by federal inspectors. If they were provincial inspectors I would not mention the subject, but in my constituency federal inspectors have been trying to get all cattle to go to the slaughterhouse instead of to the butcher's shop, thus preventing the butcher buying direct from the producer.
If it is to be the case that sales are to be conducted only in this way, with the meat first going to the slaughterhouse, you will find the price will be fixed by the slaughterhouse, which will have complete control, probably indirect but nevertheless complete, and the farmer will know exactly how much he is getting for his beef and how much the consumer will be paying for it in the butcher's shop. This means the butcher will get a rough deal. The slaughterhouse will control the price and when one buys meat from

the butcher he will have to pay the price which the slaughterhouse wants.
I should like the minister to scrutinize this point and try to prevent possible control or monopoly in the meat market, a control which is developing at this moment. The other day in the committee we asked some of the officials of the research branch what work was being done in relation to sterilized products. We were referring to sterile milk products, sterile meat and other foodstuffs. A good deal of work has been done in this field in other countries, but we were told that little had been done in Canada.
In the area from which I come sterile milk, sold under the label of Multimilk, is causing a good deal of concern to farmers, because the milk which is used is a surplus product selling at about $2.80 a hundred. It goes into northern Ontario and meets competition from fluid milk at about $5.15 a hundred. So there is a great difference between _ the reward the farmer gets for his share in the production of these two products. I think there would be less complaint if those concerned were bringing in fluid milk from the London area. It would still cause concern, but transportation costs would be an important factor in determining the final price.
If the farm organizations had known the potential of this sterile milk product before it began to enter the area, the farmers would never have allowed it to come in. They would have done the advertising necessary to counteract its sale. They would have been prepared, if necessary, to pool their milk resources and supply a similar product, presumably under another name, as a secondary product. In any case a competitive system would have been established.
I refer in particular to Timiskaming and the surrounding area, because this is the area where the product got its biggest try-out.
I know it is possible to buy Multimilk in Ottawa as well as in other parts of Ontario. There is an argument going on around this product at the present time. The federal Department of Agriculture so far has not been able to decide whether the sterile milk is actually a processed milk product, such as reconstituted whole milk, or whether it is condensed milk and therefore a secondary milk product. This is an important question as far as the farmers are concerned because it means a 100 per cent difference to them in. the prices they receive.

Supply-Agriculture
I presume the minister has some knowledge of this problem. I suggest the farm organizations should at least have been given some information about this process. I am not saying the department should get mixed up with the negotiations in the districts and in the divisions which are being conducted within the industry. Ontario has had more than its share of heartaches in this respect. But it is not too late even now to do something about this situation. The department has been carrying out extensive research with regard to the extension of this sterile product patent to various other foodstuffs, including meat. In the United States a steak can be wrapped in ordinary, clear paper and put on a shelf or a table for two or three weeks, without refrigeration, and at the end of that time the meat is still in a satisfactory condition for human consumption. There are, however, some reservations to be attached to this. The process kills most of the bacteria which cause deterioration. Milk does not turn sour and meat does not go bad. But the process is not capable of destroying all the types of bacteria which may be present, and the product may still not be fit for human consumption.
There is another point which I wish to bring to the minister's attention. Many housewives can go into a store and buy cream- this is quite a complaint recently-that has an additive so the cream does not go sour. But the cream becomes very blue or light in colour. When you pour it into coffee it does not curdle, but the taste is something out of this world and anybody smelling it would probably not bother with cream for some time. This additive is not illegal, but in my opinion some research by the department is warranted because we are now entering upon completely new technological developments in the handling of dairy products.
I was surprised when the director of the research department said that cream with such an additive had not been investigated. It may be that the amount of the estimate is not high enough and more people should be added to that branch. I am sure they are very capable in their field of research, but I think the farmers have the right to be forewarned and to have some advance knowledge of the technological advances that are taking place, because this is vitally important to the operation of their marketing agencies and the method by which they control the distribution of their production.
I am not sure whether the federal government is going to look after this field or whether it is the provincial people, with some of whom I had the opportunity of talking the other day. However, I believe there is an obligation on the federal Department of

Agriculture to do the necessary research so that before any change in the product takes place the farmers will have the opportunity of knowing that such a change can be made.
I am sure you personally, Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as you represent a constituency with a very large dairy industry, are aware of the developments that have been taking place in the last few years in the use of bulk tanks and other methods of handling milk. Milk is no longer collected from the farms every day but rather several times a week in the winter and perhaps more often in the summer. This type of milk handling has resulted in very large credit outlays on a fairly long term basis, and the farmers are encountering a great deal of this in the operation of their farms. It seems to me that when a large truck can come into an area and have enough milk under light refrigeration to supply that particular area, this is a hazard that the farmers should have been warned about so they might have been able to do something about it.
I do not imagine this matter can be decided today. I am not demanding that the minister give an opinion on it or express any indication that it is going to be examined, but I strongly urge that the minister at least consider it. It is a new and large field. In my view it is going to play a considerable role in eastern agriculture in the near future, and if the federal government wants to make a greater contribution than it has been making probably the cheapest way they can do so while at the same time providing the most assistance to many farmers would be in the field of research.

Mr. Chairman, with regard to vote No. 90, I have received, as I am sure the minister has, many representations asking

whether the original intention of the federal government in making available grants to the class A and class B fairs could be extended to the class C fairs, because the class C fairs would appear to be doing more for agriculture than either the A or B class fairs. I do not see the fairs listed here, but one of the A class fairs, I presume, would be the national exhibition. Then there is the royal winter fair, the eastern Ontario agricultural fair. I believe they are B class fairs. C class fairs are those little fairs that are held throughout the agricultural communities across the nation which allow farmers to show farm livestock for exhibition purposes, vegetable displays, farm crafts and the other aspects of farming in relation to what is actually happening in a community. The A and B class fairs in my opinion-and I think this opinion is shared by many people-have gone into the exhibition class and are really trade class fairs now, rather than agricultural class fairs. The problem is developing in my own area where we have a very large C class fair at New Lisk-eard. This has reached the size now where there is constantly a great deal of pressure put on the fair board to include exhibitors who are not in the agricultural field at all; they may be automobile, manufactured goods, natural gas or any other entrepreneur. These people are asking to hold exhibitions there and exhibit their potential and their wares, rather than the agricultural people themselves.
If some consideration were given to these class C fairs, it is my opinion that these agricultural fairs would be the ones to really demonstrate the potential of agriculture in a given area. There are many small class C fairs that do a great deal of good. As an example, there is the Charlton fair in my area. It is very small. I do not know the standard for a class A or class B fair, but I suppose it has some relationship to the number of people who attend. Charlton is a small community of about 700 people, and is a fairly progressive potato growing area as well as other mixed farming.
I use Charlton as an example of what I believe agricultural fairs should do. There was a family a number of years ago who started exhibiting what I suppose were very muddy and misshapen potatoes. The judges who came from other areas to the Charlton fair told this family what the different types of potatoes were supposed to look like. As a result of this the family, by the name of Ryan, eventually was able to win first prize at the Charlton fair. They later exhibited their potatoes at the royal winter fair where they took first prize. Then, they exhibited them at the international world fair and their

potatoes brought to Canada and the little village of Charlton the world championship.
The point I am making, Mr. Chairman, is that as a result of the education process which takes place through these fairs, people can often develop products that are able to bring awards to Canada and bring esteem to our nation. The hon. member for Cochrane, of course, could tell the same story. Over a period of many years, as a result of exhibiting in small fairs, people in the Cochrane district have been able to develop a wheat crop that has won the world championship. The same process has been repeated with other products.
The point I am making is that when you have people winning these awards who originally exhibited at small regional fairs, this shows the value of the small class C fairs. I am sure the minister is familiar with this problem. I am quite sure he goes to more fairs than I do. I am proud of the fact that I have quite a number of them in my area. I am sure he has seen many class C fairs, the ones in which manufacturers do not ask for space, and in which the farmer exhibits the products he has worked very hard to develop. It seems to me that this is the area in which the greatest gain to the farmer would be derived. The farmers who start exhibiting in class A and class B fairs probably never reach the top. Those who start in class C fairs very often develop products that win awards. These fairs, therefore, are the ones that are the most worthy of support. I should like to ask the minister to really consider this matter.
There are many young people in the 4-H clubs and junior farm organizations who would like to contribute to these class C fairs. These are the ones that the federal government does not assist. I am aware of the fact that there are difficulties involved in the way of grants for buildings, perhaps scholarships, and so on. Perhaps these awards could be given to certain classes who would be entitled to exhibit at a higher level. Certainly, in northern Ontario, there is a great interest in continuing and expanding the class C fairs. I should like the minister to consider this matter very seriously because it seems to me this is one way in which he could help to develop a better type of agriculture both in relation to animal husbandry, plants and grain.

I should like to ask one question on this item. It is a complicated question because it involves dominion-provincial responsibilities. Will the minister consider, or has he considered, the extension of the subsidy on lime used as fertilizer? There are many areas in which the cost of fertilizer varies according to transportation costs. It appears to me and to farm organizations as well that the fairly farsighted policy regarding agricultural lime, if applied to the use of fertilizer for agriculture, would bring a return to the farmers which in my opinion would probably be out of proportion to the cost the government would incur in making this subsidy. The farmers union of Ontario have asked for this on numerous occasions. The farm organizations themselves have asked for this. Their submission, which I think is a reasonable one, is that lime used in agriculture is only required for specific conditions. Farmers in one area need lime, while others do not. There are other supplements which could be added to the fertilizers on other farms which do not use lime but which would be as beneficial as lime.
I was wondering whether the department had considered the matter and were prepared to make some recommendations to the provinces at the next federal-provincial agricultural conference so as to ascertain what assistance the provincial governments would provide. I believe leadership has to come from the federal government, owing to our subventions, but I think the country would be interested to know the minister's thinking on whether this type of assistance can be extended. As I say, lime applies only to some farms, whereas nitrogen and other chemicals have a wider application and can serve a somewhat similar function on land on which lime would be unsuitable. Mr. Chairman, just one or two remarks on vote 130 which deals with the administration of the board of grain commissioners. I want to make an appeal to the minister. There was a recent change in the regulations regarding the definition of an elevator which would qualify for licensing. At the present time the act says:
"Elevator" means any premises into which western grain may be received, or out of which it may he discharged, directly from or into railway cars or vessels-
[Mr. Herridge.l
This definition precludes the giving of a licence by the board of grain commissioners to any off-track storage. At the present stage of railway abandonment I know that my asking for a change in the act is not very popular, because the present definition of the communities with elevators alongside "elevator" certainly strengthens the case for any railway track that it is proposed to abandon, and this provision in the act also strengthens the case for the elevator companies. While it is not very popular to take this position at the present time, I firmly believe that some of the railways in western Canada are going to be abandoned, whether this year or five years from now. I also believe there are a lot of elevators situated alongside railway tracks which could serve a very useful purpose to the neighbouring communities, even if the railway was abandoned. For example, at several places around Medicine Hat almost all the grain coming into the elevator is taken out again and hauled to the mills by trucks. So paying large subsidies to maintain some of these railways, simply on the pretext that they are necessary for the movement out of the elevators of grain, when in actual fact the railway is not even used for that, is to me just a nonsensical approach.
One of the first things necessary in my opinion is to make some small amendments to the Canada Grain Act so that these elevators could remain licensed by the board, even though the railway alongside had been abandoned.
I do not want to labour the point now, but I think it is necessary that the government recognize, and that the board of grain commissioners recognize, that some of these elevators could serve a very useful purpose even when the railway is not there. For one thing they could be gathering points for the farmers in the immediate area, who could bring in small amounts of grain and sell it. On the other hand, if the railway is abandoned -they would have to haul the grain to the mill themselves. When the elevator is full and the time comes for the grain to be shipped out, it is a well accepted practice now to send a fleet of trucks to empty the elevator. But as long as this provision remains in the act, then if the railway is taken away the elevator goes too.

I should like to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm. There is a growing demand that eastern Canada should be shown some of the consideration which has been given to western Canada under P.F.R.A. and other agencies. It seems to me that removing this item and placing it under ARDA is nothing but eyewash. We, in the east, may get a few of these projects, but only at the wish of the province.
Farmers in eastern Canada need the benefit of some of these projects which have been developed in western Canada and which have proven to be successful there. I believe that in dealing with eastern agriculture the federal government should not divorce itself from some of the responsibilities it has assumed over the years with respect to the western provinces. I do not intend to press the point further at this time. But I think that the minister and the department should take warning that some of us representing eastern agriculture are not going to be quiet another year on this matter. We are not asking for the discontinuance or curtailment of anything in this regard in western Canada, but we are going to ask for equal treatment in each of these fields in eastern Canada. If the department wants to get along well with us they are going to have to make some concessions.
Personally I am not interested in the department saying these things are going to come under ARDA. If ARDA is interpreted properly by the department, they are going to have to face the fact that is a long term project to convert much agricultural production into other fields of endeavour. I think this is fairly fundamental. It is not a short term but rather a long term solution for agricultural problems. The provisions that are made under this item and following items should also be made applicable to eastern

Canada in the same way they have been applied in western Canada, and the ARDA program should not be restricted to eastern Canada because of certain fundamental changes in agricultural production such as mentioned by the previous speaker in relation to fodder, which have been accomplished under some of these grants.
I should like to have the minister's opinion on whether or not he is prepared to give consideration to the extension on equal terms to the eastern provinces, of some of these projects now under way in the western provinces, which projects are administered and supervised by the federal government and not in co-operation with the provincial government. I believe, as many others do, that there is a field in which co-operation is necessary, but there is also a field in which the federal government can give leadership and I suggest that the experience gained from these projects undertaken in western Canada should be applied to the undertaking of similar projects in eastern Canada. I think the minister should indicate now whether he intends to extend these projects into the eastern areas and whether or not this will be brought about by the time the minister presents his next estimates.
