Mr. Chairman, when my estimates were previously considered by this committee on October 24 last I agreed to make a statement on the question of participation by the Soviet union in the conference on north Pacific fisheries. Opinion has been expressed in some quarters, especially by the leaders of the maritime fishermen and allied workers union that the Soviet union should be brought into the convention with Canada, Japan and the United States covering the fisheries of the north Pacific ocean. The hon. member for Skeena brought this subject up in the course of the debate on these estimates on October 24.
First of all it should be pointed out that the Canadian government would be glad to co-operate with the Soviet union in the management of sea fisheries. Canada and the Soviet union are now parties together with the United States and Japan to the interim convention on conservation of north Pacific fur seals. The Soviet union as well as Canada is also a party to the northwest Atlantic fisheries convention, along with 11 other countries. It is hoped that this cooperation in the development of sea fisheries can continue and be further extended.
However, in the fisheries of the north Pacific, in which Canada is interested, these being principally salmon, halibut and herring, a special situation exists, perhaps unique in the world, in that these fisheries have been developed either singly or in some instances jointly with the United States to the point of full utilization, based on scientific management at great national cost over a long period of time.
It was because of this unique situation that the north Pacific fisheries convention between Canada, Japan and the United States provided for the reservation of these fisheries to the nations which have developed them, and Japan agreed voluntarily to abstain from fishing for salmon, halibut and herring of North American origin in the high seas where normally there is freedom of fishing for all nations.
The Soviet union, whose fishing fleets and operations have been greatly expanded in the last decade has so far given no indication that it would recognize the special or unique situation of our fisheries. On the contrary the Soviet union has publicly proclaimed it is against the principle that any nation or group of nations can reserve for their own use the fisheries in the high seas.
Supply-Fisheries
At the 1958 Geneva conference on the law of the sea, Mr. Krylov, a delegate representing the Soviet union, made this statement in the third committee:
The principle of abstention was at variance with the principle of equality of rights and the concept of freedom of fishing on the high seas. In the U.S.S.R.'s opinion no discrimination should be allowed against relative "newcomers" in fishing grounds already being exploited by other states.
This attitude of the Soviet government was further confirmed in an exchange of notes between Canada and the U.S.S.R. in 1961-62. On October 4, 1961 the Canadian government, being apprehensive of the effect on our highly conserved fisheries, of expanding Soviet fishing operations in the north Pacific, sent a note to the U.S.S.R. in which it pointed out the long and painstaking efforts of Canada and the United States in the preservation of the halibut of the north Pacific ocean and expressed the hope that the Soviet union would co-operate in avoiding any damage to this resource by its fishing operations.
In a reply dated February 12, 1962 the Soviet government said that it cannot agree with the attempt by Canada and the United States to question the right of other countries to fish halibut in the open seas and that the U.S.S.R. could not recognize the monopolistic rights of Canada and the United States in the area. The Soviet note added that the Soviet fishing organizations are not at present conducting large scale halibut fisheries in the northern part of the Pacific ocean; that operations are limited to the study of reserves, the habitat and the seasonal migration of halibut. The note ended by stating that should the Soviet government in the future begin commercial fishing in the area it would be ready to co-operate with the governments of Canada and the United States on a just and equal basis in the protection of halibut reserves and in the regulation of its catch.
So far there has been no indication of any change in this attitude of the Soviet government. Therefore, there would be little likelihood of getting the co-operation of the Soviet government in obtaining the protection of our salmon, halibut and herring resources to the extent now obtainable under the convention between Canada, Japan and the United States
Representations are from time to time made by the leaders of the united fishermen and allied workers union which also find their echoes here in parliament that the Soviet union exploits its salmon resources in the same way as Canada and the United States, that is, at the surf line, and the Soviet fishermen do not fish for salmon in the high seas. The same people argue that because of this the Soviet government would support the

Supply-Fisheries
Canadian and United States position: that for the proper management of salmon, high seas fishing should not be permitted. Those who argue that way overlook the fact that the Soviet union and Japan have a separate treaty on salmon fishing in the northwestern Pacific. Under this treaty the right of Japan to engage in salmon fishing in the high seas is recognized, and at the annual commission meetings a quota of Japanese catch of salmon is set for each year. In fact, far from restricting Japanese fishing in the high seas, Japan is restricted to fishing only in the high seas at considerable distances from the coasts of the Soviet union. Therefore the question of Soviet participation is one for consideration by Canada, Japan and the United States. Perhaps the attitude of the Soviet government may change in the future and it will be prepared to cooperate in recognizing the unique situation of our salmon, halibut and herring fisheries, and that these resources, being fully utilized, need special protection under the principle now incorporated in the north Pacific convention between Canada, Japan and the United States, or a similar principle. The situation may also arise where if the Soviet union should exploit stocks of fish which are of concern to us on an economically significant scale and to our disadvantage, we may have to conclude that the best solution would be to bring the U.S.S.R. into the agreement. In such case Canada will consult with Japan and the United States on the matter. At the present time, however, for the reasons I have given, the time is not opportune to initiate any further discussions on the subject.
This concludes the statement which I had in mind in connection with the participation of the U.S.S.R. in the north Pacific fisheries. In their note which was tabled the other day the U.S.S.R. make it very clear that it cannot recognize the monopolistic right of Canada and the United States to exploit the living resources of the open seas in the northeast part of the Pacific ocean.

Mr. Chairman, I think it is quite evident to everyone that if the minister had had the foresight and interest to make such a statement when his estimates were being considered earlier, perhaps they would have been passed at that time. It is this sort of full declaration of support for the action, or lack of action, of a government that is appreciated by the house and by the country. It has cleared up a number of misunderstandings. All this difficulty developed because of the hesitancy of the minister to fully disclose what was in his mind and in the mind of the government. There was threaded throughout his statement very slight, but none the less they were there, insinuations which could be interpreted by members of
[Mr. Roblchaud.l
the house as being directed toward them. 1 do not want to take that interpretation in so far as I am concerned. I will say, however, that it is a good thing for the country that the individual fisherman and the groups of fishermen find a voice in the House of Commons, for there is no question that the fisheries association finds its spokesmen here in parliament, and I think to bring it into balance it is necessary that all sides of the case are put forward.
I was very interested to read the exchange of notes between Canada and the Soviet union regarding the halibut fishery which was, as the minister said, tabled, not at my request but upon an order of the house, really, even though I initiated the motion. I was likewise interested to see that at the time of that order of the house to table this particular correspondence, an admission was made that there was no such correspondence in existence with respect to either of the five species of salmon which intermingle in the midPacific, or with respect to herring; but only with respect to halibut. I do not want to be accused-although I am sure many people would like to do this; perhaps may even do it regardless of my contention here-of being the spokesman on behalf of the government of the Soviet union or the government of any other nation; but I think, in order to have all the information on the record, we should read fully the note from the Soviet union with respect to the halibut fishery so we can see that not only did the Soviet union contend in that note, as the minister said, that it would not recognize the monopolistic right of Canada and the United States to exploit the living resources of the open seas in the northeast part of the Pacific ocean, but the Soviet union also makes reference to their attitude about conservation.
This is from sessional paper 269, which reads as follows:
The following is a translation of the text of the Soviet ministry's note dated February 12, 1962 and numbered II/2E in reply to the note of October 4, 1961 from the Canadian ambassador in Moscow.
It reads as follows:
The ministry of foreign affairs of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics presents its compliments to the Canadian embassy and with reference to the embassy's note of October 4, 1961 concerning the halibut fishery in the northeast part of the Pacific ocean has the honour to declare the following:
Then it says:
The Soviet government cannot agree with the attempt, contained in the note, to call in question the right of other countries to fish halibut in open seas of the northeast part of the Pacific ocean. The existence of a bilateral agreement between Canada and the United States of America concerning the regulation of halibut fishing in the northern part of the Pacific ocean and in the

Bering sea, to which the Canadian government refers, cannot be an obstacle preventing other countries from fishing halibut in the above mentioned region. It is known that, according to the generally accepted norms of international law, high seas are open to fishing by all states. The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics therefor cannot recognize the monopolistic right of Canada and the United States of America to exploit the living resources of the open seas in the northeast part of the Pacific ocean.
It is fairly clear that their contention is that the high seas are open to anybody subject, however, to any treaties which may exist. I cannot help but compare the attitude expressed in that paragraph which I have just read with the attitude the United Kingdom took to poor little, insignificant Iceland when it took steps to declare a 12-mile fishing zone, when they put warships and everything else out to protect what Great Britain contended was its right under international law. None the less, that is the attitude expressed in this note by the Soviet union. I think any country which has that attitude and carries it into full effect, without regard to the detrimental influence it may have on other countries, is committing something that is unconscionable. I think, in this regard, while the Soviet union in one sense may be correct in its reference to what it thinks are the accepted norms of international law, none the less the language is far too strong for my liking and carries with it the implication, "If you do not agree with this and if we desire so to fish there, other methods will be instituted to guarantee our right to fish the resources of the high seas". The note goes on to say this:
The government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics always proceeds from the need for international co-operation between states in the matter of the rational conduct of fisheries in order to maintain the productivity of commercial fish in the open seas at a constant level, while permitting the maximum permissible catch.
I do not think there is any disagreement with that statement. I think it is the kind of statement Canada would make, although I would have one reservation about the use of the word "constant" where the note says:
-in order to maintain the productivity of commercial fish in the open seas at a constant level-
I think the desire in all approaches to exploitation and conservation is not only to maintain the productivity but to see whether the productivity can be increased. Therefore with the exception of the use of the word "constant" and the desire to substitute therefor the attitude of increasing productivity, which is I think our goal, this is a statement with which I am sure the Canadian government agrees. I am sure the Minister of Fisheries has, in fact, made precisely the same sort of statement, perhaps not using
Supply-Fisheries
those exact words. He nods his head in agreement, so I take it that is an agreeable statement and that the Canadian government shares the attitude referred to, namely that we should always proceed from the need for international co-operation between states in the matter of the rational conduct of fisheries, in order to maintain the productivity of commercial fish in the open seas at a constant level, while permitting the maximum permissible catch.
Then, I should like to read the last paragraph of the Soviet union note:
At the present time, Soviet fishing organizations are not conducting large scale halibut fisheries in the northern part of the Pacific ocean.
I think the same condition exists today, and they are not engaging in the halibut fisheries.
For the time being, these operations are limited to the study of the reserves, the habitat, and the seasonal migration of the halibut. If in the future the Soviet government decides to begin the commercial catching of the halibut in the above-mentioned region, it will be ready to co-operate on a just and equal base with the governments of Canada and the United States of America in the protection of halibut reserves and in the regulation of its catch.
While the note from the Soviet union starts off on a note of arrogance and disdain for what I consider the legitimate claims of Canada to protect that which we conserve in co-operation with the United States, it winds up in a declaration of co-operation. I think that note should be put on the record so that a clear picture is there for those who want to read it and who will appreciate the situation. I did not feel it would be necessary to read the original note from Ambassador Smith in Moscow to the Soviet union dated October 4, because, in essence, what it says is that "the Canadian government is concerned about your activities in the northeastern Pacific, and we would like you to consider our situation." However, I thought it was necessary to read the note from the Soviet union in its entirety and express my thoughts about it as we proceed.
The Soviet union is not now, so far as we know, as the minister said, engaging in salmon fishing on the high seas, at least not in that area of the mid-Pacific where the salmon from both sides would meet. I think they are engaging in the salmon fishery, but that would be closer to their own shores. I do not believe it really matters a great deal whether or not the Soviet union is in a treaty with us regarding herring, because our herring fishery is a relatively close offshore fishery. If the position of the Canadian government to the effect that we should have a 12-mile fishing limit is adopted and the boundary is drawn in such a manner as to include

Supply-Fisheries
Hecate strait, Queen Charlotte sound and Dixon entrance, then we do not have to concern ourselves too much about inroads that would be made into our herring stock, because they would be almost entirely within our own waters. We would then have to concern ourselves only with those that spawn off the Queen Charlotte islands, and those have been removed from the abstention principle so far as Japan is concerned.
It is our salmon fishery that is of interest and of concern. In regard to the salmon fishery, I should like to quote from a publication entitled "Western Fisheries", for November, 1963. This issue contains a report on the recent meeting of the north Pacific fisheries commission in the latter part of November, wherein the Bering sea halibut quota was reduced by a little more than 40 per cent. There are some interesting references here to this particular question. I should like to read a comment by a United States delegate, namely Mr. Clarence F. Pautzke, commissioner of the fish and wildlife service and head of the United States section. At the opening of the plenary session of the commission he said:
The commission failed to take adequate steps at its last annual meeting for protection of the red salmon runs of North American origin which are exposed to the Japanese fishery west of 175 degrees west longitude.
Perhaps I am guessing now, but I think the reference to red salmon would be a reference to the sockeye species. I continue to quote from the article:
"The Bristol Bay run (in 1963) was smaller than was expected," Pautzke said. "The information available to the U.S. indicates that the Japanese fishery took a large proportion of the run. The run which entered Bristol bay was so small as to cause a disaster in the industry in the United States.
Had the commission taken timely action, the situation would have been better.
This should not be permitted to happen again. The commission must do more than it has in the past if it is to maintain any semblance of responsibility," Pautzke warned.
That is the end of the quotation, but the article then goes on to say:
This was the strongest formal statement to come out of the meeting and reflects the grave fears of the industry in Alaska that the salmon runs of Bristol bay may be facing extinction under the pressure of the Japanese ocean fishery, and the mounting concern for other fishery resources, especially king crab and halibut, which are coming under rapidly increasing exploitation by Soviet fleets.
This article says that the halibut and king crab fisheries are coming under rapidly increasing exploitation by the Soviet fleets. Already the United States people are concerned about the possible extinction of the salmon run in the Bristol bay area as a result of the expansion of Soviet fishing activities,

and the king crab and halibut fisheries are also under pressure. I think that if such is the case it should cause us concern.
There is no question but that the pressure of the population has forced nations to look to the sea for a greater amount of their food, especially protein products. It is quite apparent that the north Pacific fisheries are already under pressure from the Japanese. This gentleman has been expressing his thoughts at the discussion which took place in respect of the attempt to renegotiate the north Pacific fisheries treaty when Japan brought pressure against the fishery stocks of the Pacific upon which we have spent thousands and thousands of dollars in attempting to conserve. The publication "Western Fisheries" makes a reference to the fact that the Soviet union is increasing its fishing activity and it refers specifically to the king crab and halibut fishery. There is no question but that the amount of pressure from the Soviet union will increase as the years go by. The pressure will increase more and more as far as those species of fish which are spawned in our land, and on which we spend countless thousands of dollars over the years in an attempt to conserve, are concerned. An attitude of complacency, an attitude of regret, an attitude of interpreting the remarks of the Soviet union to the effect that it is not interested in international co-operation or conservation on the high seas is not good enough. It is true that the Soviet union's note of February 12, 1962, as I said, was arrogant, disdainful and disgraceful in its first part, where it interpreted the norms of international law as meaning it could not care less about what Canada does in the matter of conservation.
The Soviet union's claim that the right to fish the high seas, while in essence and under international law perhaps correct, in actual fact is, as far as I am concerned, despicable. We know that the Soviet union are masters of speaking with two voices; of saying one thing one time and something else another time. Nevertheless the contention of the Soviet union in the latter part of its note is that it will be ready to co-operate. Let me read the words again:
If in the future the Soviet government decides to begin the commercial catching of the halibut in the abovementioned region, it will be ready to co-operate on a just and equal base with the governments of Canada and the United States of America in the protection of halibut reserves and in the regulation of its catch.
Then in November 1963 "Western Fisheries" says that the king crab and halibut are coming under rapidly increasing exploitation by the Soviet fleets. If that is the case I think it is high time that we got down off our diplomatic horse and dealt man to man and face

to lace with the Soviet union, and say to them point blank: "If you guys are going to fish on the high seas, fish which we spend thousand of dollars to conserve, then you had better get into a conservation treaty with us. We want you to come in with us". We should not wait until it is too late, until the size of the fleet of the Soviet union is such that not only will the salmon runs be subject to extinction, but all other runs as well. The time to move is now. I sincerely hope that the minister gets a little closer to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, fights for this action in the cabinet, and takes some steps to deal with the Soviet union in an open and direct way in an attempt to save our fisheries from extinction. That is the matter of prime concern to people on the west coast, particularly the fishermen, and it should be of prime concern to the people in the rest of Canada as well.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to prolong this discussion unduly but I am sure the Minister of Fisheries would be the first to agree that what happens on the high seas in fishing matters is one of the most important matters which can be discussed in the fisheries field. I think the quotation referred to in this communication from the Soviet union, in particular the phrase which says that it is known that according to the generally accepted norms of international law the high seas are open to fishing by all states, is a contention which has been promulgated by many other nations as well as the Soviet union. It is important that we should recognize that that attitude arose at a time when it was assumed that the fish on the high seas were wild fish. I think there is a parallel in the hunting of wild game. If we go to the areas of our own plains in the days when the buffalo roamed, the buffalo were wild game and fair game for all comers. The time has come when Canada should be promulgating new doctrines of international law in respect to fishing on the high seas.
I think we should take a stand which has its parallel in the law of the range, where in effect certain cattle owners put their brand on their herds. I think we should be raising our voice to put the Canadian brand on some of the fish now roaming the open range of the high seas. The time has now come when there should be a new approach in the field of international law to this matter so that it is clearly recognized that the fish which in effect are reared within our borders, and which for the time being are out on the open range, under any proper understanding of international law are our fish. This is a revolutionary doctrine, I think it would be agreed. But I think it should also be agreed that our scientists are doing some rather revolutionary
Supply

Fisheries
things in fisheries and in the field of fish rearing. This calls for a new approach to international law.
The fact that we have these votes in our estimates to support certain international commissions is an indication that we have taken some steps in this direction. But I suggest that at this particular stage we should, through the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, be sounding forth with a much clearer voice than we have been the promulgation of this new concept in respect of those to whom the resources of fish on the high seas belong. I think this is more important to the question of the survival of Pacific salmon fisheries than it is to any other fisheries matter at the present time.
I think it should be evident that the great concern that is felt by almost everyone I have met in the coastal areas of British Columbia who know anything about fish, and the changes made to the north Pacific fisheries treaty annex is basically due to a growing appreciation of the need for insisting that those fish which go from our shores into the high seas temporarily to feed are really Canadian fish.
As the minister knows, I have expressed concern about this matter in a motion which is still on the order paper, and which I doubt will receive very much further discussion during this session of parliament, in respect to the manner in which the government dealt with the amendments to that treaty. My concern about the manner in which they were dealt with is basically due to the fact that I feel it represents an attitude on the part of the government of Canada which fails to recognize how important a public question is the manner in which these treaties are amended. It is not good enough. At a time when we should be seeking to gain acceptance in the international field of a new concept relating to resources of fish on the high seas it is not good enough for us to agree to amend and change treaties in a way which gives the impression it is done under the carpet or under the table.
In closing I submit that this parliament and the people of Canada have still not been informed in any official way that I know of that the treaty has been changed. I can find nothing in Votes and Proceedings about it. I can find nothing in the Canada Gazette. As far as I know, nothing has appeared in any of the official channels through which the government of Canada gives notice that certain actions have been taken. I mention this matter on the discussion of these estimates because I feel it is symbolic of the government's failure to appreciate the importance of what it is doing with respect to these changes

Supply-Fisheries
which are being made in the north Pacific fisheries convention, in particular, and other conventions which, we hope, will be developed so that we may have a new concept and a new acceptance of international law on the high seas, a concept which will in many ways differ to such an extent from that initiated in this document sent by the Soviet union to our government as to be a complete reversal of the attitude which is here expressed.

It will be difficult for me to give an explanation of the figures which have been quoted by the hon. member for Skeena. The hon. member will realize, however, that such figures may not give a true picture of the situation because only two years have been selected, 1952 and 1961, and in order to give a true picture we should have the catch year by year. It is true that Japan has increased its activity in salmon fishing, especially in the last decade, and this could explain the increase in the catch of salmon by Japan by 264 million pounds. As the hon. member has mentioned, most of this fishing, in fact, probably all, is done on the high seas.
In so far as the advisory committee is concerned, I promised the hon. member when he asked me a question some time ago that I would give a report on my estimates. The advisory committee to the Canadian section of the international north Pacific fisheries commission held its second meeting at Vancouver, November 15, 1963, under the chairmanship of the deputy minister of fisheries, Dr. A. W. H. Needier. Members attending this meeting were Mr. Francis W. Millerd, fisheries association of British Columbia, Mr. Homer Stevens, united fishermen and allied workers union, Mr. Martin Eriksen, Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative association and Mr. R. Stanton, Pacific trollers association. Messrs. J. M. Buchanan, J. C. Cameron and Carl Giske, Canadian members of the international north Pacific fisheries commission, the area director, W. R. Hourston, and Dr. W. M. Sprules, special assistant to the deputy minister, also attended.
There was a frank exchange of views regarding problems to be considered by the annual meeting of the international north Pacific fisheries commission, November 18 to 23, especially joint conservation measures on halibut in the Bering sea, measures to prevent trawling for other bottom fish from damaging halibut stocks in the gulf of Alaska, and the continued qualification of stocks of salmon, halibut and herring for abstention by Japan. Progress in the negotiations of a revised north Pacific fisheries treaty with Japan and the United States and the objectives to be sought in continuation of these negotiations were also discussed.

In the meantime I wish to advise the hon. member that an application has been received from the Grand Harbour co-operative, Grand Manan, for a subsidy and the application has been approved by the Department of Fisheries and the Department of Agriculture. A decision by treasury board is expected soon. It may have been made this afternoon. I have not had any report yet.
Another group has had some communications with my department about a subsidy but they have not decided whether they will make an application.

I should like to express my appreciation to the minister for disclosing that information to the committee. It would indicate that while there is a so-called freeze on subventions the freeze is quickly thawing, and at least one application has been decided upon favourably. I anticipate one other application coming to the attention of the minister very shortly.

Yes. In fact, I had a discussion about it this afternoon with the representatives of the group concerned. I would ask my colleague, the Solicitor General, to move:
That vote No. 50 be reduced by $70,000.

speechtext:
We hope the minister will make a very short statement.
Hon. J. R. Garland (Minister of National
Revenue):	I shall be delighted to oblige
in the short aspect of it. The estimates before the committee are those covered by votes Nos. 1, 5, 10, and 15, and they provide for the financing of the 1963-64 operations of the customs and excise division of the Department of National Revenue. I should point out to the committee that these estimates are quite separate from the estimates of the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue and I would ask the committee's cooperation, as in past years, in keeping the discussions of them separate. It seems past experience has shown that more orderly and effective discussion is possible in this manner.
These customs and excise estimates total $40,571,400 and do not include some $2,341,000 supplementary moneys provided for the most recent revisions of salaries. Of course, as members of the committee know, salaries make up most of these estimates and in fact account for more than 93 per cent of the total.
A great deal can be said about the operations of this division which last year was responsible for collecting $2,397 million in customs and excise revenues. However, in view of the rather tight schedule of the committee I will limit myself to saying that in the short time I have been Minister of National Revenue I have been greatly impressed by the efficiency and forward-looking spirit which I feel characterizes the policies of the administration of the customs and excise division.
The record bears this out. It shows, for example, that last year, 1962-63, the total of revenue collections was close to $470 million more than was collected in 1958-59. The

record shows also that during this period almost every area of customs and excise operations experienced considerable development and growth. Yet, notwithstanding these additional demands on its resources and staff, the customs and excise division has during this period, through good management actually reduced its personnel establishment. At the commencement of the current fiscal year this division had 518 fewer employees than it had five years ago, which represents an annual savings of over $2 million. Such is the record of the administration of the customs and excise division, and I think that it speaks for itself.
I shall be pleased to do my best to answer any questions that hon. members may wish to raise, and I again would ask their co-operation in considering the customs and excise division separate from the taxation division. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether the committee would permit me to inject a personal note here. I would like to express my thanks -this is the first opportunity I have had to do so publicly-to my predecessor, the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, for assisting in the smooth transition following the change of government and the take over of this department.
Hear, hear.

I would also express the hope that I might enjoy, in the passage of these estimates, at least some degree of the success that was enjoyed by another predecessor, the very able, well respected hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
I have a few words to say about certain administrative procedures in the income tax office of my riding-

I gladly agree with your suggestion, Mr. Chairman.

Taxation division-
20. General administration, $3,906,300. [Translation]

Mr. Chairman, I come now to some remarks I want to make about the
Supply-National Revenue income tax office located at Rouyn, in my riding of Villeneuve.
As in all the other income tax districts, naturally, methods are being used which I believe may not be known to the minister himself but which are certainly known to his officials. I am thinking here of those tyrants, those zealous men who seem to be envious of those who succeed and who take pleasure in torturing them with very little reason or no reason at all by making them believe that they will be severely punished by the income tax division if they do not conform to their rules. Hence, those officials misuse their authority and act with arrogance.
I had a personal knowledge of actions by certain inspectors of the income tax in the division of Rouyn-Noranda, which comprises the whole northwest region of the province of Quebec. Let me give you a name. One Mr. Bob Hardy, for instance, is an inspector who checks the bookkeeping and takes pleasure in fining small businessmen because they do not send to the department, at the required date, the amount collected from their employees as income tax. He even threatens to send them to prison if they do not send their cheques at once for the tax collected and this, on top of the fine which is imposed.
This Mr. Hardy is a big man and he seems to be all-powerful in his department. Therefore, I vigorously protest against the actions of those federal employees. If the officials of the division know about such things, a man such as Bob Hardy of the Rouyn division, should be made to toe the line and be called to order.
I also would like to call the minister's attention to the matter of charity receipts, about which the minister has probably heard.
The figures of charity receipts submitted to the minister have been cut down, particularly since the present government came to power. Last year, and the year before that, we met with much less difficulties; but this year, it seems that everybody is acting in collusion, to harass not the taxpayer who, is not bothered in his own home, but rather the parish priest who is being disturbed at his residence, and asked to check his books, in order to certify whether Mr. So-and-so has given $100, $200 or $50 to charity. Then, in a most arbitrary manner, the authorities cut down the total amount of the charity receipts which the Canadian taxpayer was able to deduct from his income tax return.
I know of several cases in my own county, where people had charity receipts for a total figure of $500 or $600, and where the income tax officer in Rouyn, on his own authority, and without consulting the taxpayers, brought down those figures by $400 or $500, and

Supply-National Revenue stated that he had established that $200 and no more had been given to charity. How could this income tax officer know what went to charity, and was given by the taxpayer?
There is a way to remedy the situation and forget altogether about charity receipts. The minister could decree a general abatement of the income tax for charity, up to 10 per cent of the personal income. This would stop the harassment of Canadian citizens by income tax inspectors.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to point out another matter to the minister. When people send in their income tax returns a few days after the deadline, the department automatically fines them. Is that logical? I find it strange then that the department has never thought of paying some interest to taxpayers who are entitled to a refund. These people may wait for weeks, or even months, before getting their refunds, but they are not granted any interest, for the government does not pay fines. After all, these taxpayers are deprived of a part of their income for a given period of time, but woe to the taxpayer who does not send in his income tax at the date set by the department, for he will certainly be fined. I see the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) shaking his head. If that does not happen in his riding, it does in mine and I am quite sure that it does happen in his riding.
It is because the member for Edmonton West never meets his electors.

The hon. member for Lapointe is probably right on that point.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wished to make. Something has to be changed in the administration of the Income Tax Act. For instance, employees of that department should show more courtesy when they meet the taxpayers.
Mr. Chairman, those inspectors are not our employers. They are government employees. They are at the service of the Canadian people and they must respect the human persons they have to deal with. Therefore, those civil servants should be a little more courteous towards the Canadian taxpayers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Athabasca.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make just a few brief remarks after complimenting the minister. It is very refreshing to have a minister begin his estimates by generously acknowledging his predecessors. This is one way in which I am certain he can expect, and will receive, the full co-operation of the house. Mr. Chairman, I would like to bring


in a private bill, if necessary, to assist our school teachers across the country in the way of providing them with some exemptions from income tax. This is of course impossible under the rules, so I just bring to the attention of the minister and his officials this very important subject.
Most of our teachers all across Canada are anxious to upgrade their own academic standing and so be in a better position to train our young people in the very competitive world in which they find themselves. In order to do this, often at great sacrifice on their part they are obliged to re-enter university. Some of them have to go back to university and attend summer school for a period of eight or ten years in order to get the qualifications necessary to be able to teach our young people in this ever-increasingly technical world. I should like to suggest that every consideration be given to the granting of a tax exemption of a reasonable amount to school teachers to cover their tuition, books and perhaps their maintenance during the summer months when they are obliged to go back to university.

Mr. Chairman, only a few words to remind the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) of a request I addressed him during the fall concerning many taxpayers in the east of the province of Quebec who have to send their income tax returns to the Montreal office and who always eagerly wait for a refund of the tax they overpaid during the year.
I noted that after representations by the minister, the civil servants of the Montreal office did speed up the revision of files. But numerous family heads have been particularly anxious in the last couple of weeks to receive the tax refund they think they are entitled to and I hope that the minister, with his recognized and proverbial kindness, will ask once again the civil servants in his department to speed up the revision of files so that the taxpayers can get the tax refund due them at least before the end of the year.

Mr. Chairman, just a few brief comments.
I too wish to come back on this matter of receipts for charitable donations since, in the Quebec area and in my constituency especially, many complaints have been made on this subject.
If I am not mistaken about the provisions of the Income Tax Act, taxpayers may deduct, for charitable purposes, up to 10 per cent of their taxable income. This means then that a person who submits a receipt in proper form, signed by the religious authorities or

the organizations to which the donations were made, can deduct up to that amount from his taxable income.
Now, such receipts are often rejected, in whole or in part, by income tax officers. If the idea is to refuse to grant deductions for these charitable donations, the thing to do is to amend the legislation. But, at this time the act allows a tax deduction up to 10 per cent of the taxable income, for charitable donations.
Moreover, I believe that the investigators, under the act, do not have a legal right to reduce claims for charitable donations, putting forward various excuses for doing so.
What is even worse is that when somebody complains, the answer is that the case was studied, that inquiries were conducted and that it was finally established that the amount to be claimed for charitable purposes did not reach the amount appearing on the receipts.
Mr. Chairman, I am not able to prove the contrary, but I would really like those officials to actually prove that they conducted an inquiry, that they did get the exact figures, since, after all, those figures can come only from those who have submitted them.
Consequently, if the receipts indicate a certain amount, I cannot understand how the investigators can state it is otherwise, or that the amount claimed was not paid.
Mr. Chairman, we receive numerous complaints to that effect, particularly in the Quebec district. That is why I wanted to call the attention of the house on this state of affairs, which is becoming a sort of tragedy. Some other procedure should be found.
The hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) suggested a method a short while ago. I believe there are no doubt others. In fact, somebody has already suggested a reduction on the tax rate for the first taxable amount of $1,000, so that the taxpayers could, without receipt, benefit from abatements almost identical.
Mr. Chairman, another problem on which I wish to call the attention of the house is that of small industries manufacturing products which are called seasonal products. The industry itself is not seasonal, but the products are.
For instance, let us take the case of the manufacturers of gloves, mitts, boots and slippers. Those manufacturers accept orders during most of the year, but as soon as they have accepted the order, they must pay the federal sales tax, according to the regulations of the Department of National Revenue. However, that sales tax is not refunded to them
Supply-National Revenue until the bill is paid, that is not until a period of at least six months, or even more, has elapsed.
There are many such industries in my constituency, considerably several of which manufacture various leather articles. The directors of those industries are obliged to bear for six months at least, sometimes longer, the cost of the federal tax which they must pay at the time of the order and which is refunded to them only when the bill is paid.
Mr. Chairman, this procedure, I think, affects the development of those small industries which we claim we want to help but which are prevented from surviving by similar things like that.
Mr. Chairman, I sincerely believe that the Minister of National Revenue should be able to change the legislation in order to remove all the economic harassment the small industrialists are subjected to at this time.
I have already contacted the officials of the Department of National Revenue about this and I have been told that it was difficult to determine the marginal difference between small and large industries. I admit that, but it should be possible to set a criterion which could be based either on the number of employees or the number of working hours, it does not matter which. This is a problem which it is up to the officials to settle. As far as we are concerned, what we want is results. We do not want small businessmen to have to wait months for the refund of a sales tax they had to pay in taking an order.

Mr. Chairman, first I want to say that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) is possibly the nicest and the most pleasant Canadian citizen I have had the pleasure to meet. And I say this not to flatter him but because I believe it. However, I must add that I doubt there is a more unpleasant department than the one he heads.
To be head of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration that is encouraging. To administer the Department of the Secretary of State, that is also encouraging. But to be Minister of National Revenue, to be the boss of those who empty our pockets, that, Mr. Chairman, is a very thankless job.
And I must say that the minister deserves all our sympathy.
I must also confess that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) chose the present Minister of National Revenue, he chose one of the nicest and most charming members to fill that most thankless job.
Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I must recognize that I have no reason to complain about the attitude of the revenue officials in my riding or my district because we have none. There is no district income tax office in

Supply-National Revenue the Saguenay-Lake St. John area. There is none in such towns as Jonquiere, Alma, Ro-berval, etc. In fact, the nearest office is in Quebec city, which means that taxpayers of my region have to travel 135 miles if they wish to submit a claim of some sort to the income tax people.

You are better off than we are, because we have one.
The hon. member for Villeneuve says that they are better favoured than we are because they have one. But I must admit that even though they are in Quebec, the inspectors are efficient enough to come and grab it. But when they want to protest, taxpayers find it far. I say that the people of Saguenay-Lake St. John are in an inferior position when it comes to appealing against the decisions of the Department of National Revenue, dispute its decisions, try to obtain information, let their opinions be known.
I recognize that the farther we are from taxation inspectors, the better it is; nevertheless, it is sometimes convenient to have them near us in order to let them know what we think.
Mr. Chairman, the only thing I should like to point out tonight is the question of charity receipts. It is well known and even striking- the minister must admit it today-that the legislation is ill conceived. Something should be changed in the act. As a rule, a 10 per cent deduction is granted to those who file charity receipts, but we ought to remember what Christ said: let not thy left hand know what your right hand does; in other words: make charitable donations but do not proclaim it on housetops.
Now, with the Minister of National Revenue, receipts are needed; everything must be in good order. Just try and make a charitable donation to an organization that is not recognized by the department or to an individual who needs it badly and is not recognized either; then it is not accepted. In my opinion, it is distorting the true meaning of Christian charity as it is usually understood. I see that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Cho-quette) approves what I am saying now. All that means only one thing, Mr. Chairman; the act is defective and should be revised.
One good solution would be to do away with this business of receipts and give a general rebate of 10 per cent on the first $3,000, for instance, 7J per cent on the next $2,000 and 5 per cent on incomes of more than $5,000. That is the first point. We must change this antiquated and immoral act which goes against all principles of true charity.
It should not be forgotten either that, under the present legislation, unjustified investigations and inquiries are being made in rectories and religious establishments.

The parish priest and his assistants are not employees of the Department of National Revenue; they are not there to represent them, but to help their parishioners and devote themselves to parochial tasks. Therefore, it is a practice that should disappear.
Those inspectors of national revenue are arrogant, Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member for Villeneuve has said. Not that they are so personally, but because of the legislation of which they are the servants, and because of the zeal which they display and the stale atmosphere which prevails in the Department of National Revenue. It would seem that everyone who works for national revenue feels an obligation to be arrogant and contemptuous to the highest possible degree. I say again that those inquiries in the presbyteries must cease.
In conclusion, I should like to ask something of the Minister of National Revenue. At the present time, a great number of constituents and taxpayers of our ridings have been writing to us along those lines: We submitted receipts of $500 or $600 for charitable donations and the department replied: Your receipt for charitable donations has been reduced to $250 or $300. We then write to the income tax office in Quebec city and always get similar letters from the same official by the name of Audette saying: After inquiry, it has been found that the individual had not donated more than such an amount.
I ask the Minister of National Revenue how can an inquiry be made when a person holds a receipt signed by the parish priest, if nobody bothers to go and see the taxpayer.
In my opinion, there is no inquiry at all or simply a superficial one that cannot be taken into account. I would therefore ask the Minister of National Revenue:
1.	To amend the legislation.
2.	As regards past cases, to instruct his inspectors to go and see the taxpayers who protest, so they can prove their good faith. In the case of those who do not protest, it means that they agree with the merits of the assessment made by the Department of National Revenue. Otherwise, it would not be an investigation but a farce.
Mr. Chairman, this is all the more important because the Income Tax Act is entirely different from all other Canadian acts. Under Quebec's civil code, a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a doubt. On the other hand, according to the Income Tax Act, a person is presumed guilty, and it is up to him to prove himself innocent beyond the shadow of a doubt. In such a case, the individual himself has to pay the costs, to hire a lawyer to prove his innocence.
Mr. Chairman, in the great majority of cases, rather than spend money to prove their

innocence, the taxpayers prefer to let the matter drop, which does not prevent them from saying: there is the kind of justice we have in Canada. And they keep on cursing the government, protesting against injustice, against the fact that they cannot assert their rights without having to spend a great deal of money.
Mr. Chairman, I maintain this is a serious matter in a democratic country where each and every one is entitled to justice and fair play. With the Income Tax Act, we do not have such a thing in Canada because the individual is first presumed guilty. Judgment is taken against him and he has to pay court expenses and lawyer's fees in order to prove his innocence.
This situation has to change, otherwise we shall see an increase in the number of Canadian citizens who will accept, without abdicating however, to be deprived from their rights because they are not prepared to spend money to have them recognized. The Income Tax Act which says that everyone is guilty unless proven innocent, must be changed.
That is what I wanted to say, Mr. Chairman. I made my remarks in good faith, I think they are pertinent and the Minister of National Revenue should inquire with his inspectors in order to find out the feeling and the climate in which they work, so as to remedy the situation and revise this legislation which is faulty in many cases.
I wonder whether the minister would have the names of institutions, organizations, etc., listed as charitable for purposes of income tax assessment set out in Hansard?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Order paper.
Do I understand that the discussion on item 1 is completed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If the minister intends to reply to the several speeches which have been made, perhaps we could recognize, before he does so, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to support the view presented by the hon. member for Athabasca with regard to allowing deductions for expenses incurred by teachers who are taking courses, not only the cost of tuition itself but of the textbooks required. I believe last year I attempted to move an amendment to that effect which was ruled out of order. I think the department has probably received representations from the Canadian teachers federation and other interested bodies with regard to this matter. This is a question of
Supply-National Revenue investment in training and efficiency, and I should like to see some consideration given this matter.
There is another matter I should like to raise for consideration by the minister and his colleagues in the cabinet. This concerns a rather important policy question. We have heard from the Liberal party in the past some suggestions about campaign expenses incurred by political parties. I do not have with me the book "The Liberal Party" by J. W. Pickersgill-usually one can get from that a quotation on any important policy matter- and I do not know whether he deals with this subject, but I should like to suggest that the cabinet give consideration to allowing certain sums of money to be deductible-that is, with respect to contributions to political parties. I think the amount would have to be in the neighbourhood of $200 or $300. Citizens who help finance the campaigns of political parties are assisting the democratic process and I think this should be recognized to a certain extent. This matter has been mentioned in the house before, but nothing seems to happen in this connection. I believe that if a lot of people could be encouraged to make contributions to political parties in the same way as they are encouraged to make contributions to charity, some of the abuses which now occur in the field of political contributions could be avoided.

I am pleased that the minister comes from northern Ontario because I am sure he will be aware of many of the problems we have there. I wish to add my voice to those who have already discussed this question of donations, particularly to religious organizations. I have had several letters from clergymen in my area who are concerned about the issuing of receipts. I have one letter from a clergyman who is being asked to list cases where donations of $1 have been described as donations of $10 and so on. He says he is not getting this money, though he and his church would be very glad if he were. Yet pressure is being put on him as if he were an employee of the people who are asking for receipts. He is being asked to supply receipts for money which he has not collected.
This is a growing problem and we shall have to face it in the future, because many more people today are earning an income which encourages them to enter religious donations, whether actually made or merely contemplated, on their tax forms. The fact is that clergy are being asked to do something which is dishonest. I suggest that workers who make a straight contribution to income tax out of their pay, without much chance

Supply-National Revenue of other deductions, are finding that this is an agreeable method of obtaining tax relief.
On the other hand, there are those who make donations to charity and ask for nothing but an honest receipt. Yet in some cases such receipts cannot be given because of the manner in which the donations are made. The donations which are put into collection plates on Sundays are difficult to account for. I am sure that if the inspectors in the department went into some of these churches and added up the receipts and related them to the collection on the plates it would be found that many people had arrived very early and that there would be no receipts for those who had arrived late. It may be, as the hon. member for Lapointe said, that it would be better to allow for the reduction of a flat sum in the case of everyone who wished to make a contribution to a religious organization. It is not a revolutionary idea because this is now being done in the case of union dues. Lodge or union dues can be deducted up to a fixed amount. I believe it would be fairer to those who now have to issue these receipts if deductions were made possible in this manner.
I am not one of those who believe that inspectors should not go round to check the information given on the tax forms. I think they should. I do not believe anyone should get a receipt for money that is not given, and I believe this has happened on many occasions. But I agree it is difficult for anyone to say with accuracy how much a parishioner has donated in a particular year unless the donation is made in a lump sum, and I imagine that this is something which seldom happens.
A point has been raised in connection with teachers' salaries and I agree that special provision should be made for those in the teaching profession who are engaged in training. It is obvious, of course, that the salary paid to different groups of teachers will vary widely and some difficulties are bound to arise as a result. I imagine that in some cases two groups of teachers could be found in the same institution whose incomes and tax responsibilities would vary widely.
Again, in conclusion, I urge the minister to look carefully into this question of tax receipts for donations. This problem is growing because of the change in our economy which has arisen with the development of the industrial age. People are earning a living in a different way. Those engaged in farm work were often in the habit of writing up a good many expenditures as farm expenses. Industrial workers have found it difficult to obtain similar advantages and this has led them, in many cases, to apply for receipts in respect of religious donations which may


never have been given. The longer we leave this question in abeyance, the more difficult it is likely to become.

Mr. Chairman, I would like here to say a few words about charitable receipts. The matter has been raised already by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) as well as the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). However, I do not share their views in that respect.
We are not surprised.

It is just that I feel there is a way to control charitable receipts with regard to income tax.
I can tell you that it is accepted where I come from; we have Catholic and Protestant parishes as in all the other ridings in the rest of Canada and we do not have any difficulty simply because we use envelopes.
When a parishioner makes a donation to his parish through this system of envelopes, or any other donation, the receipt he receives for the amount given in the envelope is the only amount he can claim as a deduction.
This is not the business of the government.

The exemption for charitable donations is an exemption under the Income Tax Act. We are already granted an exemption of $100 without receipt. If you examine the situation in general, you will notice that less than 35 per cent of parishioners who pay taxes, require a receipt. First, there are the children and the persons who have no job; then there are those whose income is not high enough to be taxable.
So the only persons who ask for receipts are those who have a taxable income, that is a third of a parish, this is no phenomenon. So why not use a system of contributions through envelopes?
That system has been used for years in dioceses in the west, and is used more and more in dioceses near the east. And I can tell you, following my experience at the Department of National Revenue, which dates back three years ago, that that system has been set up in some dioceses of the province of Quebec, and it works.

I should like to raise now certain points I have raised from time to time in the past with regard to the administration of the department. The first one has to do with the allowance for the use of an automobile for business reasons, whether by lawyers, automobile salesmen, travelling salesmen, farmers or anyone else. If my memory serves me correctly, a farmer may be allowed 75 per cent of his automobile expenses when the automobile is used for farm purposes. Automobiles are no longer in the category of a luxury or

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words in connection with corporation taxes as compared with personal income tax.
It is a well-known fact that taxpayers pay 22J per cent as income tax. The percentage is worked out for each $100. For example, the taxpayer who has a net income of $1,000, pays 14J per cent of income tax covering the difference between $1,000 and $2,000 and this percentage increases up to 80 per cent.
On the other hand, companies pay 22J per cent on the first $100 of income up to $35,000.
I think that there is a serious discrimination here against taxpayers as compared with companies. That is why I ask the minister to examine carefully that situation so that justice may be done in this regard, especially when one considers that individuals pay more taxes than corporations do.
Besides, corporations are entitled to reinvest capital while individual persons are denied that right.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on behalf of the worker. We all know that, to earn their living, workers need the tools of their trade. For instance, bush-workers need many mechanical tools that cost a great deal of money. But the cost of those tools, unfortunately, is not deductible for income tax purpose and, as a result, the workers have to pay for those tools themselves. What is more they even have to have cars to carry them to their work, so they can earn a living. Neither their car nor their tools are exempt from income tax.

Consequently, I think the minister should give this matter serious consideration in order to treat the workers a bit more fairly.
I would like also to talk about the carpenters. They also need many tools in their line of work. I can also mention the plumbers who find themselves in the same situation. The cost of the tools used by these skilled workers cannot be deducted either for income tax purposes.
I submit that the Minister of National Revenue should consider all those cases and I ask him to study carefully the situation of those poor workers, those poor people who work hard to earn a living and do not benefit from any exemption for the cost of the tools they need to earn a living.
That is all I had to say, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, from the music we are hearing tonight there is no doubt we are hearing Christmas, and to hear the minister sing the praises of the former minister is certainly reassuring. I was glad to have the minister put on record that he did not want to take any credit away from his predecessor with regard to the technical training measure. It was certainly reassuring to hear him say that he wanted to pay a special tribute to the hon. member for Ontario for all he has done to prepare our young people to be better equipped for the future. I again thank him for putting this on the record and I wholeheartedly agree with him.

Item agreed to.
45. Administration ot the Government Employees Compensation Act, $114,000.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member rising on vote No. 45?

Yes. Several problems have come to my attention in relation to the federal compensation act. I know the minister has been very busy with labour matters that he is not normally called on to deal with, but I am sure he has given consideration to some of the problems that will face us with the new areas that are to fall under the jurisdiction of the federal government. The establishment of two new territories in northern Canada will add to these problems and I believe the time has arrived for the

federal government to provide some leadership in establishing for those areas a model compensation set-up that will be a guide for them when they achieve the status of provinces.
I receive letters about many compensation cases in Ontario and some from Quebec and I was very surprised when I received one a few weeks ago from a workman in Frobisher, who had been home for some time with a broken leg, to find that he was receiving no compensation. I was particularly surprised because in this case the matter of compensation was being handled not by the federal government but by a trust company in Montreal. It seems to me we are going backward a long way when we have trust companies dealing with compensation matters.
We are aware of the difficulties that have arisen in the Northwest Territories in relation to employees there and the fact that in public works contracts it is specified that the Department of Labour will only deal with those cases arising out of works that have been declared to be in the public interest and for the public good. It is surprising, but there are officials in the Department of Labour who will say that a vote of this house providing for a particular project in the Northwest Territories does not qualify that project to be considered to be in the interests of Canada. I would presume that gentleman must be a Conservative now, with a Liberal government, and had been a Liberal previously, with the Conservative government, because he seems to be very perverse in this regard. He is not alone. The Department of Justice and many other departments were involved in this particular case and none of them could come to the conclusion that I thought should be reached. But this does raise the point that there is a great deal of difficulty in establishing jurisdiction in that area.
While this other case was in another labour field the fact that this man had an accident and that it was a compensation case confirms that the whole field needs some examination. I know this is not a large item and that in the whole of Canada employees, including public service employees, are very cautious and safety conscious. An item of less than $3 million a year is not a significant one. However, I would think the minister might like to institute a pilot compensation set-up under federal jurisdiction in order to provide legislation that would assist provinces who might wish to look to Ottawa to bring their own compensation boards up to date.
I believe that in the past it has been necessary to use provincial compensation boards, hospitals and other facilities, but now that we are establishing new areas under
Supply-Labour
federal jurisdiction I think a federal compensation board would serve a purpose not met by any other agency. Therefore I think the minister should consider establishing a model compensation board under federal jurisdiction. The fact that as far as the territories are concerned it would not be in existence too long is no reason to restrict it, but an added incentive to make it as good as possible, so that when provincial compensation boards are established they can take advantage of the farsightedness of the federal government.
I am not expecting the minister to suggest that he is prepared to set up this type of compensation board, but I submit he should give some consideration to it. When the bills to set up the two new territories in northern Canada, the Eskimo one and the other, are brought forward it is my intention to try to have compensation boards established if the federal government has not moved in that field before these territories are established. I suggest that the minister should consider the matter, and if this can be done I am sure the people in these areas will certainly appreciate it.

Item agreed to.
50. Administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act, $45,412,500.

On a previous occasion the minister said that some 362 new positions were being added to the national employment service. Have these been approved by treasury board, and when does he anticipate they will be filled-in a year, a year and a half,, or two years?

The additional personnel have been approved by treasury board. We are actively recruiting now through the civil service commission, and we want to fill the positions just as quickly as the commission gets the people for us.

I had the experience when we tried to fill 175 positions in the area of placement officers that it took something well over two years before they were all filled. Are these positions in respect of placement officers?

There is a considerable number of employment officers in the establishment and there is provision for special service officers, if that is the term, who would take a more active part in manpower development, training and retraining programs of the employed and unemployed, and who would assist generally in the promotion locally of manpower programs. My hon. friend will appreciate this is a pretty important activity, and that is why we would

Supply-Labour
like to get the recruitment done as quickly as possible. It may be that it will take us longer than we expect and that we will have the difficulty experienced by my hon. friend when he was minister.
How many of these positions are placement officer positions?
The large share of these 362 are employment or placement officers, and maybe 100 for other categories.
About 100 out of 362?
Roughly 250 placement officers or employment officers.
What is the present state of the unemployment insurance fund, when does the minister expect it will be depleted, and is he making any provision for a loan?

At the end of November the amount in the fund was roughly $56 million. We have already made provision for the usual loans, so that we expect we are fully covered for the present fiscal year. It may be we will have a deficit but we are in a position to deal with it.
