Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the house has a rather heavy program and that everyone is anxious to be on holidays, I shall not repeat what I said a while ago. But, even if I wander a bit from the item before us, I do wish to tell the minister how much I would appreciate it if the job opportunities advertised by the various employment offices were given more elaborate publicity.
Employment offices receive from the Department of Labour, through the usual channels of distribution, notices of job vacancies and they try to bring those opportunities to the attention of workers in the area.
I am wondering whether employment offices are giving enough publicity to such notices so that the unemployed may be made aware of them.
On that matter, I should like to give the example of an office which makes known its employment offers as they should be made known. It is the office of Three Rivers which, I believe, could be held up as a model for all other offices in the province as regards the publicity it gives to the employment offers and the means by which it makes things easier for the unemployed who call at that employment office.
I should like to see all other offices in the province follow the example of the Three Rivers office in order that the unemployed be well informed about the different job opportunities.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say just one thing about item No. 50 to the minister responsible for the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Section 21 of the act, general principle, says:
That any employment Is insurable, except those exempted under the terms of the act.
Consequently, a little further in the act, there is a long list giving all exempted employment, including agricultural employment.
The act does not say anything more about agricultural employment. In my opinion, that is dealing a bit harshly, even unjustly, with people who would like to do agricultural work. Therefore, I submit that the act should be amended to enable agricultural employment to become insurable because farmers have a hard time finding farm hands.
Many cases have been submitted to me by farmers in my riding, to the effect that they encountered great difficulties in securing farm help because they were not covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act. I therefore consider that this exemption of farm employees mentioned in the list appended to section 21 of the Unemployment Insurance Act should be amended so as to provide for the coverage of those farm hands by the act.
That is the only remark I wanted to make. [Text]

That would be a good question for the minister to answer, because many of us want to know whether the government intends to place farm labourers under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would like to ask him, is he aware of the problem in many parts where the inspectors coming into areas to do spot checks classify certain areas as remote areas for employment.
It seems to me that if a man is employed for a period of time in a locality and is obtaining a livelihood there, it is not fair for an inspector to come and say, "This is a remote area and you will not be eligible for unemployment insurance. You are now in a category that will not allow you to draw unemployment insurance." I would sympathize with the minister if an I.B.M. operator went into a lumber area where there was no sizeable plant, and certainly no equipment. That person would be placing himself or herself in a remote area for employment purposes.
This matter has been a real problem in my part of the country; and I do not think there is any difference in an area where employment is obtained for seven or eight months of the year, and is difficult to find the other four months from, for example, those in the fishing industry who cannot go fishing in the off season, and sometimes cannot fish because of weather conditions. I am sure

this is not the general policy of the unemployment insurance office, but the outside inspectors do go into an area with the avowed purpose of knocking off 20 per cent of the unemployment insurance benefactors. I have taken some of these cases through the various steps and have in several cases gone as far as the board of referees. The matter cannot be argued satisfactorily because when it is decided that this is a remote area, the only thing that can be said against it is that it is not a remote area. Going before the board of referees cannot establish any conclusion in these cases. I would like to know whether the minister is considering this matter of remote areas and what changes he proposes to make to correct the abuses-and there are certainly abuses in some areas-in the use of the term "remote area".

Mr. Chairman, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour a subject with which he is very familiar. I refer to the matter of unemployment insurance for farm labourers. I had a bill on the order paper for a number of years, but the reason given to me for nothing having been done in the past was that the Gill committee report, when it was handed down, would make some recommendations and would contain clarification on this point. As I pointed out to the minister not very long ago, the Gill committee report is actually in favour of unemployment insurance payments being made to all unemployed people, if administrative difficulties can be overcome. At that time the minister agreed with my proposition, and said that as soon as the Gill committee report was handed down, this problem would be given serious consideration. I would like again to direct the attention of the minister to this problem, Mr. Chairman, because in my opinion and in the opinion of many people, this is a serious problem, and this is the only section of our labour force that is not covered by unemployment insurance.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, there is a brief remark I have to make. There is also a class of employees who are not covered by unemployment insurance. I refer to the seasonal provincial employees-at least in the case of the province of Quebec.
I would ask the minister to kindly consider the possibility of covering those seasonal employees who, forced to remain unemployed a few months, receive no income during the winter months.
Supply-Labour

Mr. Chairman, I was expecting the minister to answer the question raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming. I wanted to ask the minister a question about another aspect of the matter of unemployment insurance.

Mr. Chairman, as I understand the point made by my hon. friend from Timiskaming, the suggestion was that inspectors would go into a particular area and disqualify workers because they were in a remote area. It seems to me this is a practice we would want to investigate, if in fact it is occurring on any scale, or even at all; because surely if a claimant has created entitlement to benefit, and is in receipt of benefit, other things being equal he ought not to be disqualified because of his residence in a particular area, remote or not. It may be that a worker who has qualified for benefit will move from one area to another and because of that movement has restricted availability of employment, which might render him eligible for disqualification because it brings in the question of test for availability of work. But I would be glad to hear of any cases or further details, and I will have the matter examined.
Perhaps while I am on my feet, Mr. Chairman, I ought to say a word about the question of farm labour raised by two hon. members. Farm labour is not an insurable occupation at the present time. The Gill committee recommends the exclusion of farm labourers because of administrative difficulties. We expect to be considering the recommendations of the Gill committee next session when they are put into a bill, and hon. members will have a full opportunity of discussing these questions in relation to general coverage, which is another matter raised by the Gill committee.
With respect to the point raised by my hon. friend in connection with seasonal provincial workers, the commission is currently in discussion with the province of Quebec with respect to coverage for provincial employees.

Just for clarification, Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise this point. There is no disagreement with the minister in the case of a person moving into an area where unemployment is not available in his type of work. However, if he makes his living in that area, he is now being disqualified for two reasons which are very much the same. One is the question of remote area, which is usually coupled with transportation. Perhaps the minister is not familiar with how this is done. A man comes into the area and goes to the unemployment insurance inspector. He answers a number of questions which form,

Supply-Labour
in effect, an affidavit. He will be asked, "Do you have a car? Does your friend have a car? Is there a public conveyance that can take you to such-and-such a place?" Then the inspector will ask, "Isn't it true that transportation facilities here are very limited?" and the man will say, "Yes, that is true". In terms of a series of questions you can elicit almost any kind of answer. This is being done and it establishes transportation difficulties to an employment centre. This question will not be reconsidered even if the claimant moves into the town, where employment might be more readily available. The man may never have worked in that town in his type of job. By going there he may really, as the minister mentioned, be putting himeslf in an area remote from the type of employment he is capable of doing.
These inspectors have done this. I suggest they have done it for the simple reason of eliminating a number of people. It is not widespread, but I believe it has been done in a number of cases. A year ago it was being done to quite an extent. If one takes such a case to the board, it usually results in a number of C.U.B.'s being cited which those appearing before the board have no opportunity of seeing. I have appeared on a number of occasions where women were involved, and usually the C.U.B.'s that were cited referred to pregnant women, and some of the problems they had. In the cases I have had, this has never been a factor. I suggest to the minister that this practice is widespread-I can only speak for my area-and there should be a redefinition in this regard. To be fair, Mr. Chairman, I must say that on the occasions we have brought these cases to the attention of the director of unemployment insurance there has been an investigation, and a satisfactory one. I have been receiving a number of letters recently from unorganized areas in which this is again a factor. I presume this is at the direction of some of the local offices.

I should like to make a short submission on this item. My district of Athabasca contains the air base at Cold Lake. This is a very poor place for employment generally, and sometimes service personnel, artisans in the lower income brackets, find it awkward when they are moved to this air base from bases which are adjacent to large cities. They are accompanied by their wives who have to give up their jobs to go there. I realize that they do so voluntarily, but they are accompanying their husbands and find themselves involved as a result in severe hardship. They run into this difficulty referred to by the hon. member for Timiska-ming. I do not know what the solution is, but I would appreciate it very much if the min-

ister's officials could look into this problem.
I have received several letters in this regard, and I would be pleased to make my files available if necessary.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about this matter of unemployment insurance for farm labour. There are certain classes of farm labour to which quite a bit of security is attached. It would seem to me the department should try to move into that general area and provide coverage for these people. It is a fact that today people who have a job which entitles them to stamps will not take a job on the farm because they would be denied stamps if they did so. Surely, there is some rule that could be brought into play that would take care of this particular situation. I only mention it to the minister now so that if he has some recommendations to introduce at the next session, he can take this problem into consideration.

Mr. Chairman, since we are dealing with unemployment insurance, I think it is appropriate to remind the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) of the conditions of the Canadian loggers who go to work in the states of Maine and Vermont.
Following a motion for the production of papers, in September last, I received certain letters with regard to a possible agreement between the state of Maine and the Canadian government. In fact, in the last letter on record, the social security representative from the state of Maine implied that in the near future, that is early in September, an agreement might be reached between the Canadian government and the state of Maine.
We are now in December. On many occasions, we have asked questions to the minister on this matter and considering that this situation affects more than 6,000 lumbermen in the ridings of Beauce and Dorchester and a few others in the lower St. Lawrence, I feel that we are justified in expecting that the minister will tell us whether negotiations are actually under way. It should be kept in mind that lumbermen have a right to expect that this problem affecting them will be solved a little more promptly.
Mr. Chairman, it was possible to reach an agreement rapidly with our neighbours on the matter of nuclear weapons. I feel, therefore, that after seven or eight years of discussions by both successive governments, and more especially following the information provided last September, when we were given to understand that an agreement was possible, it is strange that no answer has yet been supplied as late as December.
Mr. Chairman, could the Minister of Labour tell us this evening whether the nego-

tiations which are under way will result in the signing of an agreement between the Canadian government and the state of Maine concerning Canadian forest workers?

Mr. Chairman, as has been indicated by some previous speakers the minister has mentioned the fact there will be an opportunity early in the next session to discuss some aspects of unemployment insurance. I do not believe any of us expect him to undertake a detailed discussion of the question of unemployment insurance tonight. However, there is one aspect of this question of unemployment insurance and the national employment service administration about which I should like to inquire. I am referring to the general pattern of establishing offices for the servicing of claims, and particularly the national employment service offices.
I have a feeling that there has been a rather rigid formula developed over the years since the commission has been in operation. I am wondering whether, along with that review of the whole operation of unemployment insurance arising out of the Gill report, this sort of thing could be reviewed. I have a particular interest in this matter and I should like to illustrate the point I have in mind by citing a case I have in my own constituency. I know that prior to 1957 in the planning of a public building for Campbell River, provision was made for an office for the national employment service. According to information given to me in answer to a question just before the last election, this place is still available.
I know, too, that no efforts of mine exerted in co-operation with the former minister of labour, and through him to the commission, nor any efforts of the former member for Comox-Alberni resulted in an indication of willingness by the commission to establish an office on either a part time or full time basis in Campbell River. A great many people feel very strongly that the problems of unemployment are aggravated because of the difficulty people have in reaching the employment service. This is emphasized at times by the inaccessibility of the office for filing claims. Using this situation as an example of what I am driving at, I should like to ask the minister to tell us whether there is any review of the whole question of policy for establishing employment offices under way at the present time, particularly from the point of view of making the national employment service a more useful instrument in the elimination of unemployment.

In this connection, Mr. Chairman, as my hon. friend realizes, the 28902-5-393
Supply-Labour
Gill committee made a proposal to separate the national employment service from the unemployment insurance commission, so that it could become a more effective instrument, more dynamic and more closely linked to the policies for employment programs. This whole question is under consideration, and surely one of the matters that we would want to consider in connection with the possible severance of the national employment service, is how to make the service more effective; and that obviously would entail locations. In that respect, the matter will be under review.

Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that we waited till a few hours before prorogation of the house to study such an important question as unemployment insurance in Canada. It is true that I have only a few words to say on this matter at the present time. However, a matter of this magnitude should have been discussed much earlier in the session, so that every hon. member would have had the opportunity to say what is going on in his riding concerning the administration of unemployment insurance.
Last week I received a letter sent to me from St. Jerome, in the county of Terrebonne, where there was a strike which lasted four months. During the strike employees were paid $12 a week by their union.
Finally the strike was settled. People reported at the unemployment insurance office to ask for their benefits. Then they were told that as long as 80 per cent of employees were not taken back by the industry concerned, they would not get more than what they had received at that time, that is $12 a week paid by their union.
I think that governments should have done something to help those people who had already suffered for four months in claiming the rights they were denied.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point I want to bring to the attention of the minister. I mean the treatment given to the unemployed when they report at the unemployment insurance office.
We have received numerous complaints in that respect. In some offices, people are as welcome as a dog on a putting green. They are treated like numbers. They are instructed to march like soldiers. It seems that an absolutely rigid discipline is imposed. Under such circumstances, I say to the minister that the unemployed suffer enough from being out of work and grappling with the problems of life without employees of federal employment offices and unemployment insurance offices causing them additional troubles.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
Now I would have another remark to make concerning conciliation, but since I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house so as to permit adoption of the estimates of the Department of Labour, I suggest to the minister to introduce his estimates much earlier at the next session, because otherwise, I think that we will exercise nevertheless our rights to discuss thoroughly the problem of unemployment insurance in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to make a speech this evening in introducing these estimates for the very good reason that they have been dealt with by the committee on veterans affairs, where I gave a brief presentation. My intention this evening is only to express my thanks for the excellent work of that committee, which has again carried on in the tradition which has been developed over the years. I think they have done an excellent job and I want to assure them that their recommendations, as well as those of the veterans groups which have made presentations to them, will be given every consideration when we examine and review the legislation of the department for the next year. When I introduced the estimates to the committee I said at that time that there would be two or three small amendments or adjustments in the amounts of three votes. These are not changes of principle or changes in programs; they are adjustments due to the fact that we were able some eight or nine months after the printed estimates were prepared to make a more accurate forecast and to assess the situation more accurately than could have been possible eight or nine months earlier. We will, of course, move these amendments as the votes come up.
I have not all the officials of the department available because I think most of them have been exposed to the committee. They answered all the questions which were asked at the time. With that, Mr. Chairman, I will end my remarks.

Supply-Veterans Affairs who has not had an opportunity to do anything about these recommendations.
I make these statements in condemnation ot no one except the leader of the house and those responsible for preparing the order of business. Here is a case where members of voluntary organizations have made their presentations. Members of parliament sitting on a committee have agreed with many of the proposals which were made. Now the officials are waiting for us to take the further steps that are required, and we cannot do it because of the time factor.

I have only a brief word to say, and that is in commendation of the work which this department has undertaken in the past. I wonder if the minister could indicate what plans the department has for the veterans hospital at Saskatoon?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I so seldom find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Timis-kaming that I cannot resist the rare opportunity of expressing my sympathy with the point he has made tonight, with the sole exception of his statement that his experience has been the same all through these years. I agree that the minister should make some statement with regard to the future plans of the department, based on the extensive submissions and the recommendations made by the committee.
During the period when I had the good fortune to be associated with the Department of Veterans Affairs, I introduced certain substantial changes in legislation and I did indicate that I thought one of the next steps should be a revision of the Pension Act. The present minister has been in office for several months. He has had the benefit of the committee hearings and he should by now be in a position to let us know what the government has in mind for the veterans of this country. I may caution the hon. gentleman by saying that, as far as I can gather, the veterans of Canada are not very sure what this government intends to do about some of their problems, and perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite should show some signs of activity along that line.
One of the main items which has been before veterans, certainly in these latter years, has been the benefit of the doubt section of the Pension Act. When I was connected with the department we endeavoured to correct that by persuasion. I recall a debate in the house on one occasion when almost all the veteran members of the house participated and talked about the problem of the benefit of the doubt clause. At the committee hearings this year very extensive evidence was introduced to show how that matter had been
dealt with in England where the same problem had arisen, and it seems to me that the minister, for the sake of the veterans of this country, should have said something tonight about the intentions of the government with regard to that particular problem.
Then there is that other section in the Pension Act which causes so much distress to the pension commission in their endeavour to do justice. It concerns servicemen who are now with the regular forces, or their dependants. It is a section in the act which saddles the pension commission with a problem which perhaps should not be a problem for the pension commission, but rather something that should be handled by the Department of National Defence. This again was a matter I had hoped to deal with, and had conditions not changed so fundamentally and so disastrously for the country perhaps it would have been dealt with by this time. But the responsibility now rests on the Liberal government. It is not a partisan matter.
In the one instance there is the problem affecting the veterans of this country under the benefit of the doubt clause and, second, there is the problem that concerns present servicemen and, in the event of their death, their dependants. These problems have to be recognized and faced and something has to be done about them. The minister has said nothing. Granted that these estimates were considered by the veterans affairs committee, and granted that under these circumstances the house will possibly not spend very much time on them, nevertheless in order to avoid spending too much time on these estimates a clear statement from the minister is desirable so that we will not have to ask him such questions or prod him into giving us a review of what the government's intentions are.
There is a third matter which is of very great interest to the veterans of this country. They would like to know the intentions of the government with regard to veterans hospitals. I recall that last spring when the report of the Glassco commission came out with a suggestion that the veterans hospitals be turned over to civilian use, we immediately said: Hands off the veterans hospitals. Subsequently I looked into the matter and I discovered that the officials of the Glassco commission who had written that particular section of the report had ignored the submission made to them by the director of medical services for the Department of Veterans Affairs. Under the circumstances, therefore, that report cannot be accepted as valid.
To create in the minds of our older veterans any doubt as to the veterans hospitals is in my view very unwise. I have said time and time again since that report was issued that

in so far as our older veterans are concerned nobody wants to deprive them of the services of the veterans hospitals which have served the veterans of this country so well all these years. Everybody realizes, of course, that if there is no further war, and we hope there will not be, the veterans hospitals will be available in time for other purposes, but for our older veterans of the first world war in particular these hospitals are essential. They are also essential, of course, for the veterans of the second world war and Korea, but at the moment the numbers of those veterans who require such attention is not as great as in the case of the veterans of the first world war. I am aware of all the reasons for and arguments about the extra expense involved in looking after our older veterans in veterans hospitals, where the cost per bed is much higher than it would be if they were given attention under other arrangements. I know all the arguments there; but until these other arrangements are made for the older veterans of this country, let us reassure them that their needs will be looked after in our veterans hospitals, and let us reassure their relatives at the same time.
On these three matters I have raised, which were the subject of considerable discussion in the committee on veterans affairs, the minister should say something to the house to inform us what the intentions of the government are. If he will do that I will relieve him of something that has been hanging over his head for eight months, his shabby treatment of a former member of the pension commission. But if he is not going to give us satisfactory answers on these other matters I will revive that matter. I will read into the record my cable to the Prime Minister and his brush-off reply which I have also described as shabby treatment of a veteran of the first world war. Therefore we await the minister's accounting.

There are two things I am going to say at the moment. The hon. member is perfectly right, of course that the report has only been in my hands a short time. The submissions of the association were also presented to me. I had meetings with most of these groups and, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, the matter will be under very intensive study and I am going to give these representations every consideration.
As far as Saskatoon is concerned, I am given to understand that tenders are about to be awarded for the new hospital there, so my hon. friend should have the answer to that shortly.

Mr. Chairman, there is one small point I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. It is a point that gave me
Supply-Veterans Affairs some pause when I occupied the position he now has. I refer to the matter of the retroactivity of a pension when awarded by the pension commission. I found some difficulty in understanding the principle involved, in that if a veteran applied for a pension, was examined and in the normal course of events was awarded a pension in six weeks or two months time after assessing his case, the pension was then made retroactive for 12 months. Even though the veteran may not have even considered it or had no entitlement 12 months earlier, the pension is paid as of 12 months earlier. I think this is done to compensate more or less for those veterans who apply for a pension, are turned down and then have to go through the appeal procedure which sometimes takes a year, 18 months or more to get a final favourable decision, with the result that they would be penalized, and therefore an average of 12 months was taken. I think basically as the commission now works it would be far more equitable to make the pension award as of the date of the application, rather than the date 12 months prior to the date of the award. If a man has applied and it takes 15, 18 or 24 months for a favourable decision to be reached, the entitlement in effect was as of the date of the application.
There may have been some cases that stretched over three or four years, many years ago, and the rule was adopted then because the officials felt too great a sum of money would be paid to a veteran. But if a man is entitled to it he should get it. It was a wrong principle to limit him to 12 months just because it took a long time to come to the decision which should have been reached in the first place. If a final appeal is favourable, then that means that the original decision should have been favourable. For those reasons it is my earnest submission to the minister that this rule should be reviewed and that the date of the application should be the date from which the award ought to start.

I have just two brief points to make. First of all I am a member of the veterans committee, and a very fine appeal was made by the Hong Kong veterans to that committee. I draw this brief to the minister's attention for special consideration. These veterans are the ones gravely affected by the controversial section 70 in the Pension Act concerning benefit of doubt. In my opinion any man who served in Hong Kong and was four years in a Japanese prison camp should certainly get the benefit of the benefit of doubt rule. There is a burden on those of us who did not pay in this very definite manner for our freedom to see to it that these veterans should not be put to the indignity of begging.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
In the absence of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, who is working very hard in the committee and in the house seeking a judicial review of the administrative boards in this connection, I would again like to draw the minister's attention to the presentation by Lord Denning, chief justice of England, which I believe is written into the minutes of the committee meetings. I do not think one could cite a higher authority on judicial matters, and he is quite open and free in his support of a judicial review of all points of law, whether or not an appeal is spelled out in the covering statute.

I would just like to add my voice in support of what the previous speaker has mentioned concerning Hong Kong veterans. One of the greatest tragedies of war involves those who suffer injuries that cannot be measured in terms of loss of limb or physical wounds. It is difficult for any of us to realize what those veterans went through during their years of imprisonment, and I believe there is not a single group of veterans so worthy of special consideration as they are.
There is no special item in the regulations which applies to them, but in many cases they are more worthy than some of those who probably have less difficulty fitting into the regulations. Therefore I urge that the minister give very careful consideration to the responsibility our nation owes these people who went over there, poorly equipped and probably poorly trained, to meet the type of struggle they had to take part in, and then go through years of imprisonment.
The second matter I wish to mention concerns war veterans allowances. I believe the maximum casual earnings allowed for those who are entitled to these allowances are $900 a year. In many cases, combined casual earnings supplemented by war veterans allowances do not provide veterans with sufficient to maintain the standard of living which we all agree a man is entitled to in this day and age. It would not cost the department anything to permit an increase in the maximum amount of casual earnings, and I believe this is a point very worthy of mention.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Red Deer would not like to leave the impression that the people who served in Hong Kong were poorly trained. Those regiments were organized at the beginning of the war. The Winnipeg Grenadiers, whom I knew so well, were mobilized in September 1939. They were well officered and the ranks were well trained. Their problem was shortage of equipment when they reached Hong Kong. They put up a magnificent fight against very 
heavy odds, and those who survived and suffered in the Japanese prison camps deserve special treatment from a grateful country. Vey few of them have recovered from the suffering they went through. I hope the hon. member will not mind if I just make that slight correction to his remarks, because they were a well trained body of troops and they fought magnificently.

I did not intend any reflection on the type of training or the degree of training they had at home, but certainly they were not trained for the type of fighting they had to face. They expected attack from the sea, and they had to fight an entirely different type of warfare. This is not a time for controversy over whether they were trained or equipped. The main point is that they deserve special consideration, and I think we are all agreed on that.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the debate on the estimates of the Department of Veterans Affairs, which amount to $335,000,000, I believe it is appropriate for me, like the hon. members who preceded me, to make a few remarks.
It is easy to realize that the expenditures of that department are rather sizeable, since they total $335,000,000. However, if we consider the objectives for which they are intended, we must admit that those who took part in the two world wars as well as the Korean conflict surely deserve all the consideration of the Canadian parliament and their country, for they were called upon to defend us. That is why I feel that it is certainly appropriate to pass those votes, even if they are very considerable, in order to avoid some criticisms of the department by veterans of world war I.
I am not sure whether the minister is aware of the fact that some veterans receive a meagre pension, which is not even the equivalent of 50 per cent of the present cost of living. None the less, veterans are entitled to a pension.
As for the pension itself, I do not know exactly according to what standards it is established. In any case, several veterans of my constituency complain that they do not receive enough to honour their commitments, and this, at a time they have reached old age and can no longer hold a position in view of their state of health, which was considerably affected during their service in world wars I and II. Moreover, I know of other veterans who returned from war with disabilities but who, during the first year after their discharge from the army, did not seem too badly affected as far as their occupation was concerned. Now, after three or four years

in civilian life, they find that their health is seriously handicapped and, then, they experience tremendous difficulties in being admitted to the class of veterans entitled to a reasonable pension.
I believe the minister should deal more seriously with such cases and, as far as possible, grant them a more generous pension, and this, in order that those veterans may be in a position to live more becomingly in their country. Furthermore, I submit that the department should see to it that veterans have adequate housing, because they have sacrificed a part of their life on the battlefields.
I think they should be given much more than what they get today, a preference when an administrative job has to be filled in the country. Thus, I think it would be possible to employ many more veterans who do not ask for more than to earn their livelihood. Unfortunately, their health is affected, they cannot take any kind of job. I think the department should give them priority as veterans in many areas where their energy could be used.
Now, I should like to point out to the minister another aspect of his department which I think is very important. I refer to the lot of veterans' widows. I have very often exchanged correspondence with the minister on that matter.
In my own riding, several veterans' widows are complaining today that people do not seem to be willing to heed their representations, because these widows do not know how to submit them. In brief, they do not know where they should apply for information they absolutely need in order to take advantage of the continuance of their husbands' pensions as veterans' widows.
I hope that after the many sittings of the veterans committee held this fall, numerous steps will be taken so that, at the next session, the Department of Veterans Affairs can bring forward something new to improve that act.
Mr. Chairman, I propose that item No. 25 be reduced by an amount of $250,000.

Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak for just a moment on this item. Before commencing my remarks I would congratulate the minister on his inheritance of an excellent department, excellently administered, and I hope the work that was carried out by his predecessors continues in the future for the benefit of the veterans of this country.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
Hear, hear.

Item 20 deals with medical research and education and it is noted that the amount is $419,000. The details, which are shown on page 453, indicate that for medical research itself the vote has been raised from $80,000 to $130,000. When Dr. Crawford appeared before the committee on veterans affairs I questioned him on the item of medical research, especially in the field of mental illness. To me this is vitally important, as I think it must be to many who have seen the broken minds of those men who served in Canada's wars. I first became interested in this matter early in world war II and I had occasion to visit Ste. Anne's military hospital, where one could see these men. It was depressing to see the men who had been bodily wounded, but it was even more depressing to see those men whose minds had been broken in 1915, 1916, 1917 and 1918 and who were still fighting their battles.
I became more deeply interested a few years later when a young man who served under my command and was decorated for gallantry was hospitalized at the end of the war for battle exhaustion so severe that for the rest of his life-he was then 19 years of age-until the time he dies he will remain in hospital. He was so battle exhausted that he could never go back to his home, to his family or to his friends. I would suggest that the minister should give very special thought in the future to the whole field of research into mental illness.
Dr. Hans Selye, the famous physician, is doing a tremendous amount of research in this whole field. His viewpoint is that stress and strain are the basic causes of most of the illnesses which beset mankind. If this is so, the men who served in battle in Canada's wars, have more than anyone else undergone stress and strain, and this calls for some consideration at the hands of this nation. I suggest to the minister that as the years go by his department will find that men who would perhaps have lived much longer and would have led much easier and happier lives will break down because of what was popularly known in world war II as battle exhaustion. This condition received much more humane treatment in world war II than it did in world war I, when a man who had been shell-shocked was considered to be a coward, and such men were sometimes shot as a result.
I commend this matter to the attention of the minister, and I hope that next time he presents his estimates he will be able to report to us that much more than is detailed in this vote has been spent in the whole broad

Supply-Veterans Affairs field of research into all types of mental illness, especially as it applies to battle exhaustion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I suggested earlier to the minister that if he would give a statement to the committee concerning some of the issues raised on item No. 1, I would refrain from drawing the attention of the committee to the treatment he afforded a first world war veteran immediately on taking office. The minister gave no statement. I simply record the fact that I sent a telegram to the Prime Minister of this country on May 8 to this effect:
When your government assumed office on 22 April there were two vacancies on the pension commission. A third vacancy was created on 1st May by the action of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I repeat my request for the immediate reinstatement of McKay to correct the imbalance in the representation of first world war veterans on the commission and in the representation of western Canada.
The Prime Minister replied as follows:
X am in receipt of your telegrams, one sent to London and one sent to my office here, concerning the decision of the Minister of Veterans Affairs not to renew the appointment of former commissioner McKay of the Canadian pension commission on the completion of his term which expired on April 30 of this year.
I do not believe that this is a matter in which I should interfere with the decision of the responsible minister.
I consider that to be shabby treatment of a veteran of this country who gave service in two world wars and who served in the trenches in the first world war at the battle of Passchendaele. Anyone who served at the battle of Passchendaele will understand the circumstances, and why I speak strongly in favour of this man.
More important than that, sir, is the fact that on May 17 I asked a question of the Minister of Veterans Affairs which is recorded on page 14 of Hansard and reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I should like to ask him whether he has filled the two vacancies on the pensions commission which were existing when the government took office on April 22.
The minister replied in these words:
To my knowledge there were no vacancies on the commission at that time.
This statement misled the house, because there were two ad hoc vacancies on that commission. I asked a supplementary question in the following words:
In view of the fact that there were two vacancies on the pensions commission when the government
Supply-Veterans Affairs
took office on April 22, I should like to ask the minister why he found it necessary, as he stated, to create a vacancy-
This was by way of a letter and a press release.
-when those two were in existence: and will he immediately correct the imbalance on the pensions commission and reinstate Mr. McKay so that representation may be restored for first world war veterans and for western Canada?
He replied as follows:
I have given the hon. gentleman a complete and truthful answer in writing to this question.
I maintain, sir, that the house was misled by that statement. There were two ad hoc vacancies on that commission when the minister was appointed, and he then created a third. He raised the issue of the non-representation of various parts of this country and tried to confuse the issue. I say that the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Prime Minister of this country treated very shabbily a veteran of this country who deserved better from this government and from his country.

I expected, of course, that the hon. gentleman would have carried out the threat he raised earlier, and that is one of the reasons I allowed him to. Second, I will not repeat the argument except to tell him that the statements I made were truthful and categorical and they remain so. To attempt to suggest that an injustice was done here means that, if there was, then I was only correcting an earlier injustice which took place a year before. I reinstated the balance of the commission because the hon. gentleman unbalanced it. I said that at the time. I still think that is the fact, and as far as I am concerned the matter rests there.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister said that on the first occasion-
That is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: -and he says "and the matter rests there". The veteran has been let out. The minister said there is no imbalance on the commission, that there are no vacancies. I say again that he is misleading the house. There were two ad hoc vacancies on the commission at the time he took office.

Mr. Chairman, I will not take very long to make my point. In this furore or difference of opinion which has developed between the minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, I recognize that a question of principle is involved. I felt that there should be protection against this sort of thing and I put on the order paper a bill, Bill No. C-35, described as an act to amend the Criminal Code (a purge for the king's evil). In this sense I just want to define

Supply-Veterans Affairs what "king's evil" means. A lot of members have come to me and have asked whether "king's evil" is scrofula, which is some kind of skin disease. In this particular case the king's evil is the arbitrary power of the king, in this sense the crown, to dismiss people at a moment's notice. It is a failure to renew an appointment which the incumbent might expect to be renewed, without giving notice of any kind.
Therefore I would advocate to all hon. members the purpose of this bill. If it had applied to this case it would have meant that the member whose appointment was not renewed would have had six months' notice. This is one of the things we should consider, that when any gentleman is drawn into the public service on an appointment basis, most of which appointments offer a high salary, and they devote three, five, perhaps seven years to their appointment, when a shift in government comes, for example, they may be dropped very quickly. I can think of some examples on the other side. A Mr. Buchanan was dropped very abruptly from the tariff board by the Conservative government. This often results in a tremendous shock to the person concerned. No matter what his partisanship may be, the bottom drops out of his economic base.
In considering people in the pension commission at the present time, those who were Conservative appointees, when their time ends, must expect to be dropped. But what about the man doing a good job on the commission? I am sure there are several of them doing a good job, whatever may be their political allegiance. I think the best way to protect them and to prevent the kind of situation developing evidenced by the obvious disagreement between the minister and the former minister is to put something like this bill I have proposed on the statute books, making it a requirement to give six months notice when an appointment will not be renewed. I leave this with hon. members as a suggestion, because it is quite apparent my bill will not be debated in this particular session of parliament.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF MINES AND TECHNICAL SURVEYS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I shall be brief since it is getting late.
However, I should not want to let this occasion go by without first congratulating my successor, whose graciousness is well known and who is doing such a fine job. I do not think my friends opposite will mind my saying that.
I should also like to pay tribute to the late Marc Boyer, the lamented deputy minister who passed on suddenly while I was his minister. His demise was a great loss not only to the officials who were associated with him in the department, but to the people in the Canadian mining industry who came in contact with him. A man of great competence, he was always in for those who sought the development of that important industry. We greatly deplore such an untimely death.
As for the present deputy minister and his assistant, I know that they carry out their duties with great competence, and I commend them for it.
I think that the minister has realized the importance of having within his department a supply of scientists and technicians who are second to none in knowledge among other
world scientists and who are responsible for the tremendous progress accomplished by one of our most important industries.
As the minister pointed out, the estimates now being considered have been prepared in great part by the Conservative administration, and I could hardly object, of course, to the projects covered in those estimates. But since the budget of this department relates mostly to industrial research, I suggest to the minister that he should certainly not yield to the pressures that must have been brought to bear by his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in order to further reduce his estimates. I know that the minister, who has the welfare of his departmental officials at heart, and more especially the country's development, will use his great influence, not only to maintain the estimates at their present level, but even to increase them so as to improve the outstanding services provided by the various divisions of the department.
Mr. Chairman, before I conclude, allow me to say that the department and particularly the mines branch renders important services to the mining industry. However, in my opinion, these services should be given more publicity, and this not only to enable the mining industry to make use of them, because it does so quite freely, but also in order that prospectors and small people of the mining industry from the grass roots of the mining industry, as we say, be better acquainted with the services of the mines branch.
In this connection, I agree with the proposal made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), to the effect that the department should tangibly support the very important work of the prospector because he is at the basis of the mining industry and hence of the discovery of this important source of wealth for our country. Therefore, I ask the minister to find concrete means to assist that very important category of our miners.
Mr. Chairman, I think the whole question of industrial research in this country should be reconsidered, and I would go as far as to suggest that the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, where there is a nucleus of scientists and specialists, be made the centre of all research services in the federal government. In my opinion, it is more than time to centralize those research services, and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys is the ideal place to achieve such a concentration.
If the government undertakes the re-organization of the public service, as suggested by the Glassco commission, it will perhaps establish a department of research, the heart

I should like to add one more point to the minister's consideration of his meeting with the prospectors. I appreciate that he intends to get in touch with the very active prospectors association at the lakehead. I have mentioned before that the minister of mines in the Ontario government at the present time is from the northwest section of Ontario, from the riding of Port Arthur. The minister knows him. He is a man who is very much in touch with mining developments. At the present time he is promoting a silver "come back" in our area. Now that we have two ministers of mines who come from the big prospecting country, I suggest it is a perfect time for them to get together, and I should like to ask the hon. gentleman if he would consider having a conference with the Ontario minister of mines specifically to see if Ontario and the federal government cannot devise a program which would be of mutual interest and which, perhaps, could also be applied to other provinces.
I am sure Saskatchewan, which has a program for prospectors at the present time, would be interested in joining in. The lure of the big strike, the dream of making it rich, of making it big through a mineral discovery is one of the dreams in Canada that to me is much more worth while than the idea of striking it rich in the Irish sweepstakes. I think it has real consequences for our economy. We need to do something about refurbishing the dream of a lot of men who have fallen behind the kind of scientific and technical advance that more and more is turning prospecting into something that is really in the hands of the very large corporations with great technical resources and geological experts, such as the hon. member for York-Scarborough.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the house leader three questions with regard to the business for tomorrow.
The first is, would he so arrange the business that we could have answers to the written questions, of which 60 remain on the order paper, and unless they are answered tomorrow I presume they will die there. The second question is, what legislative items are still to be considered, and will he call those first tomorrow? Then my third question is, what estimates will be taken up tomorrow?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I can propose, but it is quite obvious that is as far as I can go. So far as the questions are concerned we had questions answered yesterday-I have almost lost track of the days-yes, yesterday. I would doubt if there are many more answers available but I would be quite glad, when
Business of the House
we have concluded the estimates and sent the appropriations bill over to the other place, if the house would agree at that time to have questions called, to give any answers that by that time are available to any of the questions on the order paper.
With regard to legislation, as I indicated last night there had been some question about whether the government would have to make some suggested changes in the legislation with respect to the world's fair. We have now reached the conclusion that the proposal that is on the order paper is the one we would like to recommend to the house, and therefore we would ask the house to consider both the resolution and the bill tomorrow. There is no difficulty about that because the bill stands for second reading, owing to some fortunate Speaker's decision in, I think, 1913; but I would hope we could have the debate wholly on one or the other. I would suggest the bill might be preferable.
There is also a notice which has been put on the paper of a resolution preceding a bill which, as a result of such consultations as we have been able to have through the usual, and some more than usual channels, I believe will be generally acceptable to the house. If, when hon. members look at their Votes and Proceedings tomorrow and see this notice, they indicate that they are prepared to proceed expeditiously with it, the government would be glad to bring it forward, and I am led to believe that if it was acceptable to the house, it would then be possible to deal by agreement with a large number of private bills that still stand on the order paper.
There is no other legislation except those two matters and the private bills I referred to, that the government feels any obligation about. There are of course quite a number of public bills, and I believe there is one other private bill and, if there is any time after the appropriations bill, it has been suggested that some time might be devoted to a further consideration of that bill. That is something I personally would like to recommend to the house when the time comes.
Which bill is the minister referring to?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is a bill in the name of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Portage-Neepawa.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I stand corrected. The hon. member himself is from Portage la Prairie.
There are still estimates of nine departments to be completed and I cannot be quite sure of the order in which they will be called because one or two ministers, and particularly my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, have other preoccupations

Business of the House tomorrow of a pretty urgent character. But as I see it now, the order in which we would like to call them is first, the Department of Industry, which has relatively little left; then the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, where no items have been passed but where there has been quite an extended debate; then the Department of National Defence, most of the items of which have been dealt with, but there are a few items still standing; then the Department of Transport, most of the items of which have been dealt with but there are quite a number of items still standing; then the Department of External Affairs which of course has been considered carefully in the special committee and
I	believe was considered for one evening in the house, but in which no item has yet been passed.
There is an item left over in the department of northern affairs and we would work it in at some convenient time among the latter estimates. Then there are the estimates of the Speaker and the Department of Finance, and my own estimates which have not yet been considered at all. I think they would be kept until the last, in the order which I have given, unless there are some very strong reasons for changing the order.
When that has been completed, so far as I can see the business of the house for the session which began on May 16, 1963, so far as the government is concerned, would be completed.
The Minister of Industry reminds me that it is various agencies within his responsibility which have to be dealt with, but that the department itself has been disposed of. That is a technical correction of some importance. Whether it will be possible to do all that business in one day I do not know, but it does raise the question of what kind of hours the house is prepared to sit.
If there is no understanding about the matter we would take the public business from
II	to 1, from 2.30 to 5, and from 7 to 10.30. I think it is perfectly obvious to every hon. member that we could not possibly complete the business in those hours. I would hope, particularly now that the hon. member for Port Arthur was able to explain the king's evil to us this evening, that there might be a disposition to forgo the private members' hour, which would make quite a difference to the day.
The government would be very happy, and I do not think there would be much objection from the staff of the house, if we could agree, from the time we start in the morning-and every effort would be made to accommodate hon. members at their convenience in this, and to accommodate the staff-to sit without a break until some time in the evening when a

motion to adjourn would be made. I would certainly be only too ready to undertake that the motion to adjourn would be made not later than eleven o'clock, and certainly not later than twelve o'clock.
If that is not agreeable, perhaps we could at least have a definite understanding that if the business is not completed tomorrow we would meet on Saturday at eleven o'clock, and have the same rules apply to our proceedings as apply on Friday, except there would be no private members' hour. Perhaps I could have some expressions of view on this question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: With regard to tomorrow we are quite prepared to meet at 11 and sit continually until some adjournment hour later that evening, and our preference would be to complete the business tomorrow if that could possibly be done. We are prepared for a Saturday sitting if this fails.

Mr. Speaker, I really do not think we have any right to keep staff here from ii in the morning until 10.30 or 11 at night without a break, no matter what the Secretary of State says. Translators, Hansard reporters, messengers and others have to be on the job during that period almost continually, and I think it is a most inhumane type of treatment to impose on any group of people. I do not think it is necessary, and I am sure that the longer we have, the more some people will waste time.
I think if we follow the time table we had today, maybe if we see we are going along pretty rapidly in the afternoon we could dispose of the supper hour, but we are certainly prepared to come back on Saturday. I think it would be better to handle this with decent hours and not kill the staff, rather than try to do it all with indecent haste and have a lot of people played out on Saturday morning.

Mr. Speaker, our group has no objection at all to the sitting hours proposed by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). However, I would suggest he asks personally whether the staff has any objections. If not, I do not see why we should not go on sitting according to the schedule suggested by the Secretary of State. In the circumstances, we are ready to do it, and even to sit Saturday if necessary.

Mr. Speaker, we, on this side, are also prepared to co-operate with the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) and the government with regard to the suggested hours for tomorrow. We are assured that arrangements will be taken so that the staff may be replaced alternatively during the lunch and supper hours. Consequently, we are prepared to agree to these sitting hours

so that we may complete consideration of the estimates in order for the house to prorogue as soon as possible.
It is strange to note that the opposition to that schedule comes precisely from those who are delaying the passing of those estimates, rather inconsiderately.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if I might perhaps form a consensus from what I have heard, without trying to be invidious in any way, it seemed to me there was absolutely no objection to sitting on Saturday if it were absolutely necessary. I would like to have that clearly understood first. If that is the case, I think perhaps I might make a modified suggestion. It would be that we take one hour for lunch tomorrow, from one o'clock to two o'clock; that we take the private members' hour for government business, and that we make no decision about the supper hour at all and see what progress has been made and what the prospects are, because I think if the staff thought they did not have to come back on Saturday they would be glad to provide the services during the supper hour tomorrow. But I think there is something in what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has said, that if it becomes certain by that time that there is to be a sitting on Saturday anyway, it might perhaps be desirable to have a break; and I hope it is clearly understood that we would sit, without any question, until eleven o'clock in the evening.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are agreeable to any of these arrangements. I hope there is no impression left here that any party in this house is disregarding the staff of this institution. I am relying on the house leader to make the necessary arrangements for the staff; and if the situation becomes impossible, we will be satisfied with his judgment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that I have been observing parliament, in it and around it, for a quarter of a century. If we manage to end this session without having one day of continuous sitting, I think it will be just about the first session that has
Business of the House ever been ended without that having been done. It is not that I mind setting a precedent, if we can do it. I hope it is understood, then, Mr. Speaker, that we will meet tomorrow at eleven o'clock; we will adjourn from one o'clock to two o'clock; we will take the private members' hour; we will consider before six o'clock, through the usual channels, whether we want to sit between six o'clock and seven o'clock; we will come back at seven o'clock; we will sit till eleven o'clock, and if we have not concluded our work, we will start our sitting on Saturday at eleven o'clock and complete it, I hope, before too long that day.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask what the minister means when he says "take the private members' hour"? Does he mean take it for government business?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that the house will sit tomorrow at the times and hours suggested by the Secretary of State?
Agreed.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, there is not any pressure with regard to sitting until eleven o'clock. I hope the Secretary of State, if he says eleven o'clock, will not put up this tirade at that particular hour.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I can assure the house, Mr. Speaker, that unless the hon. member for Timiskaming rises and asks us to sit after eleven o'clock tomorrow night, I will not ask.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we should also have it noted, just to get it all together that we are agreed to the Saturday sitting if necessary.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed, as far as the Saturday sittings are concerned?
Agreed.
It being seventeen minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
